en: In the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, at the beginning of the first chapter (*ullāsa*), the author pays homage to his chosen deity, who is appropriate for the occasion, in order to dispel obstacles to the composition of the work:
Victorious is the speech of the poet, which brings about a creation free from the constraints imposed by destiny, consisting solely of bliss, independent of anything else,
and beautiful with its nine poetic sentiments.

That which is determined by the power of destiny (*niyati*), possesses a fixed form, has pleasure, pain, and delusion as its inherent nature, is dependent upon auxiliary causes such as atoms and karma, and consists of the six tastes— which are not exclusively pleasant— such is the creation (*nirmiti*) or emanation (*nirmāṇa*) of Brahmā.
The creation of the poet’s speech, however, is distinct from this.
For this very reason, [the word] "conquers" (jayati) is used;
and since a salutation is implied by the sense of "conquering," it is understood that "I bow down before her. //1//
Here, he states that the subject matter is accompanied by its purpose:

"Poetry leads to fame, to the attainment of wealth, to knowledge of worldly conduct, and to the warding off of misfortune; it provides immediate supreme bliss and, by being like a beloved woman, it is conducive to instruction. (MKpr-K_2)

It provides fame like that of Kālidāsa and others, wealth like that of Dhāvaka and others from Śrīharṣa and others, knowledge of the proper conduct expected by kings and others, and the warding off of misfortune like that of Mayūra and others from Āditya and others. It is the crown of all purposes, consisting of bliss produced immediately upon the tasting of aesthetic flavor (rasa) in which all other objects of cognition have dissolved; it excels the Veda and other scriptures—which are like masters and prioritize words—by virtue of its subordinating both word and meaning to the operation that constitutes a limb of rasa.

That poetry which is characterized by distinctiveness—the work of a poet skilled in transcendent description—draws one toward itself like a beloved by instilling a sense of aesthetic relish (*sarasatā*).

It then provides instruction, as appropriate for both the poet and the connoisseur, that one should behave like Rāma and others, and not like Rāvaṇa and others; therefore, one must strive in every way toward such [poetry]. //2//

Having thus stated its purpose, he states the cause: "Power, skillfulness arising from the study of the world, the sciences, poetry, and so forth, and practice through instruction from those who know poetry—these are the causes for its production. (MK 3)
*Śakti* (poetic power) is a specific latent impression (*saṃskāra*) in the form of the seed of poetry, without which poetry would not emerge, or if it were to emerge, it would be laughable.
[This applies to] the world— meaning the conduct of the world consisting of both the stationary and the moving—
as well as to the *śāstras*, which are treatises on metrics, grammar, lexicography, the arts, the four aims of life, and the characteristics of elephants, horses, swords, and so forth.
Mastery [of expression] arises from the critical examination of poems composed by great poets and, by implication, of the epics (itihāsas). Furthermore,
it consists in the repeated engagement in both composing and analyzing poetry through the instruction of those who know how to do so.
These three, when combined and not separately, are the cause for the arising, the creation, and the manifestation of that poetry; they are not [individually] causes. //3//
Having thus stated its cause, he declares its essential nature:
"That [poetry] consists of word and meaning free from defects; it possesses qualities, and sometimes, moreover, is without ornaments.
Defects, qualities, and ornaments will be explained later.

By the phrase "in some cases," he means this: that while it [poetry] generally possesses ornaments (*alaṃkāra*), there is no loss of its status as poetry even in the absence of manifest ornaments in certain instances.
For example:
He who ravished me in my youth is indeed that same lover; those same nights of Caitra remain; those same mature breezes from the Kadamba trees, fragrant with blooming Mālatī flowers, are still there;
and I am that very same person. And yet, in his presence, I am one who knows the playful arts of the sport of love.
"My heart yearns for the shade of the reed-tree on the bank of the Revā.
(By Śīlābhaṭṭārikā, etc.
Here, no poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is clearly manifest.
And because rasa is the primary element, it does not constitute a mere ornament (alaṅkāra).
He states its varieties in sequence:
"This is called 'Dhvani' by the wise when the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) excels the expressed (vācya). (MKpr-K_4)
"This" refers to poetry.
By learned grammarians, the term *dhvani* was applied to that word which manifests the primary manifested form of *sphoṭa*.

Subsequently, others who follow that doctrine have likewise applied it to the pair consisting of word and meaning (*śabdārthayugala*) which is capable of manifesting a suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*) while subordinating the expressed sense (*vācya*).
Just as the surface of your breasts is entirely stripped of sandalwood paste, the redness is wiped from your lips,
your eyes are far devoid of collyrium, and this slender body of yours is covered in horripilation— [it reveals that you have been embraced by your lover].
O messenger, speaker of falsehoods, who remains unaware of the arrival of suffering for your kinsmen:
you have gone from here to bathe in the pond, but not to the presence of that base man.
(Amaruśataka 105)
In this case, it is primarily by means of the word "lowest" (adhamapada) that the suggestion is conveyed: "You have gone to him alone to sport. //4//

When the suggested meaning is not of such a nature [as to surpass the literal], it is *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion), which is considered mediocre. "Not of such a nature" means when it does not excel the expressed meaning. For example:
"The village youth, whose hand was joined with a fresh cluster of *vañjula* blossoms, [was embraced by the young woman...]"
"As she gazes [at it], the luster of her face becomes increasingly pale.
(Rudraṭa’s *Kāvyālaṅkāra* 7.39).
Here, the suggested meaning—that she did not go to the bower of *vañjula* creepers where the appointment had been made—is subordinated (*guṇībhūta*).
For, in comparison with that, it is the expressed meaning alone that possesses aesthetic charm.
But that which possesses verbal beauty or objective beauty, yet lacks suggested meaning (avyaṅgya), is considered inferior.
"Citra" means endowed with poetic qualities (*guṇa*) and ornaments (*alaṃkāra*).
"Avyaṅgya" means devoid of a clearly manifest suggested meaning (*pratīyamānārtha*).
"Avara" means inferior. For example:

May [the mountain] protect you—[the mountain] where, for the sake of the daily ritual bathing performed by great sages whose delusions are dispelled by the surging mass of water that is clear, bubbling freely from the hollows of its cascades; where the trees are no longer impoverished by the long, deep caves of frogs leaping up with joy; and where the rising, noble croaking of frogs resounds through the caverns.
The Mandākinī, whose intoxication is thickened by the great waves of her overflowing pride, [attains] sluggishness upon hearing that he has emerged from his own palace even by mere chance.
(Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*) He whom she hears has emerged from his own abode, the subduer of pride, even by mere chance... [she becomes sluggish].
"Amāravatī, with its bolts cast down in haste by Indra in agitation, seemed as if its eyes were closed in fear.
(From the *Hayagrīvavadha* composed by Mēṇṭha).
Thus ends the section titled "The Determination of the Purpose, Cause, and Specific Nature of Poetry" in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*.
First Chapter (Ullāsa) // 1 // In order, he states the essential nature of word and meaning:
"In this context, the word is threefold: denotative (*vācaka*), indicative (*lākṣaṇika*), and suggestive (*vyañjaka*)."
In this context, regarding this poetry,
their essential nature will be explained.
The denoted and so forth would be its objects;
[namely] the denoted, the indicated, and the suggested.
...and the intended meaning [of the treatise] is also found in some [of these]. (MK 6)

The view of the proponents of the theory that words express their meanings independently (abhihitānvayavādins) is as follows: through the force of expectancy (ākāṅkṣā), compatibility (yogyatā), and proximity (saṃnidhi), when the word-meanings—whose specific natures will be described hereafter—are syntactically combined, the sentence-meaning, which is the intended meaning (tātparyārtha) and possesses a distinct form, emerges even though it is not itself a word-meaning.
The meaning of a sentence is indeed nothing other than what is expressed; this is the view of the proponents of the theory of the expression of the related (anvitābhidhāna). //6//

It is generally accepted that all [types of] meanings possess suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*). Here, regarding the expressed meaning (*vācya*), it is as follows: "O Maithilī, today indeed there is no one who can restrain you; this has been declared by you."
"Mother, you have established that there are indeed no household supplies today. So tell me, what is to be done?
The day will not remain thus."
In this [verse from Hāla’s *Gāthāsaptaśatī*], it is suggested that she is seeking to wander at her own will.
An example of the indicated (*lakṣya*) is as follows:
"O friend, while winning over that fortunate man, you have been distressed moment by moment on my account; yet you have acted with such sincerity and affection as is worthy of you. (7)
"You have performed an act consistent with the affection one feels for a true friend.
[From Hāla’s *Gāthāsaptaśatī*]—
here, the intended meaning (*lakṣya*) is that by delighting my beloved, you have acted as an enemy.
And by that, the manifestation of the lover's transgression regarding the object of desire is suggested (*vyaṅgya*). As for the suggested meaning:
"The crane shines motionless and still upon the lotus leaf."
Behold,
the crane, motionless and still, shines upon the lotus leaf like a conch shell resting in a vessel of pure emerald. //8//
(Hāla’s Gāthāsaptaśatī 1.4) Here,
by means of being motionless, there is the state of being at ease;
and by that, the absence of people.
Therefore, this is said by someone to someone else: "This is a place of assignation.
Or rather, it is suggested: "You are speaking falsely; you have never come here before."
He states the essential nature of the denotative word and the others in their respective order:
"That which directly denotes the object conventionally assigned to it is the denotative word (vācaka)."

Since there is no cognition of a word's meaning for one who has not grasped its convention (*saṃketa*), a word conveys a specific meaning only with the assistance of convention; therefore, that [word] for which a convention is grasped without mediation in relation to a certain [object] is the designator (*vācaka*) of that [object]. //7//
The conventional [object] is of four types—the genus (*jāti*) and so forth—or it is the genus alone.

Although it is indeed the individual (*vyakti*) that is fit for engagement or withdrawal because it performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), nevertheless, because of its infinity and because of ambiguity (*vyabhicāra*), it is not proper to establish a convention with respect to it;
otherwise, the distinction between the objects of expressions such as "cow," "white," "moving," and "Dittha" would not be possible.
The convention [of a word] applies only to its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
And the limiting adjunct is of two kinds: that which is an inherent property of the thing (*vastudharma*) and that which is imposed by the speaker's whim (*vaktṛyadṛcchā-saṃniveśita*).
The property of the thing is also twofold: established (*siddha*) and to be proven (*sādhya*).
The accomplished [category] is also twofold: that which bestows life upon a thing and that which is the cause of imparting a specific quality.
Of these, the first is the genus (*jāti*).
For it is said in the *Vākyapadīya*:
"For a cow is neither a cow by its own nature nor a non-cow;
it is a cow due to its connection with cowness.
This is the second quality.
For an object whose existence has been established by means of [qualities] such as whiteness is thereby qualified.
That which is to be accomplished (sādhya) consists of action (kriyā), having parts that occur in a temporal sequence of prior and posterior.

As for words such as "Ḍittha," their own form—which is grasped by the final cognition and in which the sequence [of phonemes] has been withdrawn—is assigned by the speaker's whim as a limiting adjunct (upādhi) to objects such as Ḍittha; thus, this [form] is of the nature of a name (saṃjñā).
Regarding the term "accidental" (*yadṛcchātmaka*):
the author of the *Mahābhāṣya* states that "the application of words is fourfold, as in 'cow,' 'white,' 'moving,' and 'Ḍittha'.
However, since atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the like are listed among the qualities (*guṇa*), their status as qualities is merely technical (*pāribhāṣika*).

Although qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*kriyā*), and proper names (*yadṛcchā*) are in reality of a single nature, they appear as if distinct due to the difference in their substrates (*āśrayabheda*). This is just as a single face appears different when reflected in various supports such as a sword, a mirror, or oil. Just as in the case of whiteness and other qualities—which, though ultimately distinct when residing in substrates such as snow, milk, or a conch shell—there arises through the power of a certain factor a non-different designation and cognition, such as "this is white, this is white," that [factor] is the universal (*sāmānya*) such as "whiteness" (*śuklatva*).

In the same way, there is "cook-ness" (*pākatva*) and so forth in the cooking of molasses, rice, and the like; and in the case of words such as *ḍittha* uttered by children, the elderly, parrots, and others—which differ at every moment—there exists "ḍittha-ness" (*ḍitthatva*) and so forth in the referents designated as *ḍittha*. Thus, some maintain that for all words, the universal (*jāti*) alone is the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). Others have stated that the word-meaning is either the possessor of that [universal] (*tadvat*) or the exclusion (*apoha*). These views have not been shown here for fear of making the book too voluminous and because they are not relevant to the present subject matter. //7//
That is the primary meaning; the primary function [of the word] toward that is called "denotation" (abhidhā).
"Sa" refers to that which is directly designated;
"asya" refers to the word. //8//

When the primary meaning is sublated, yet there is a connection [between that meaning and another], another meaning is indicated either by convention (*rūḍhi*) or for a specific purpose (*prayojana*); that which thus indicates another meaning is *lakṣaṇā*, an operation based on superimposition.

In cases such as "skilled in ritual acts" (*karmaṇi kuśalaḥ*), because the grasping of *darbha* grass and so forth is impossible; and in cases such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), because the Gaṅgā and so forth cannot possibly be the physical locus of a hamlet; since the primary meaning is thus sublated, and because [the meanings] "discrimination" and "proximity" are established through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) as the relevant relations;

and furthermore, because of common usage such as "a hamlet on the bank of the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgātaṭe ghoṣaḥ*), for those who do not understand it in that way, there is [the understanding of] "purity" and so forth.

When, due to the nature of the presentation of phenomena as such and for a specific purpose, a secondary meaning is indicated by the primary meaning, that superimposed operation of the word which rests upon an intermediate meaning is *lakṣaṇā*. (9)
The throwing of one's own [meaning] to another for the sake of establishing it, and the surrendering of one's own [meaning] to another for the sake of another;
these are called the two types of pure indication (*lakṣaṇā*), namely "appropriation" (*upādāna*) and "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*). // MKpr-K_10 //

In expressions such as "the spears enter" (*kuntāḥ praviśanti*) or "the sticks enter" (*yaṣṭayaḥ praviśanti*), persons who are in conjunction with the spears and so forth are implied for the sake of establishing the entry of the spears themselves.

Therefore, this is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by means of a material cause (*upādāna*). In cases such as "a cow is to be sacrificed" (*gaur anubandhyaḥ*), the individual is implied by the genus (*jāti*) so that the binding enjoined by the sacred scripture might come about; however, it is not expressed by the word itself.

According to the maxim, "The denotative function [of a word] cannot reach the qualified object once its power is exhausted in the qualifier," the metaphorical indication based on inclusion (*upādāna-lakṣaṇā*) should not be cited here;
for there is no purpose [for it], nor is this a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).
Rather, because an individual is invariably concomitant with the universal, the individual is implied by the universal.
Just as in "let it be done" (*kriyatām*) the agent is implied,
in "do it" (*kurv*) the object is implied,
and in "enter, [eat] the cake" (*praviśa piṇḍīm*) and so forth, [the words] "house" and "eat" are respectively implied.

In the case of "The fat Devadatta does not eat during the day," nocturnal eating is not indicated by either *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption from what is heard) or *arthāpatti* (presumption), because that is the specific domain of those two. In the case of "A hamlet on the Ganges," the word "Ganges" surrenders its own primary meaning (*svārtha*) so as to establish the bank as the locus for the hamlet; in such instances, this is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by means of indication.
And this [indication] is of two kinds and is "pure" (*śuddhā*).
Because it is not mixed with figurative usage (*upacāra*),
there is no form of external neutrality (*tāṭasthya*) between these two— the indicated (*lakṣya*) and the indicator (*lakṣaka*).
For when banks and the like are conveyed by words such as "Ganges," it is through the apprehension of the actual identity (*tattva*) that the intended purpose is fully realized.

If, however, there were only the cognition of a mere connection with the Gaṅgā, then what would be the difference between this and the primary denotation of the word "on the bank of the Gaṅgā" (gaṅgātaṭe ghoṣaḥ), as opposed to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā)? //10//
But another is the *sāropā* (superimposition-based), where both the object and the subject are stated as such;

that is, where the thing being superimposed and the locus of superimposition are indicated in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) without their difference being concealed, that is *sāropā* indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
When another object is made internal [to the metaphor], that [metaphor] would be sādhyavasānikā (one in which the object is superimposed).

When the object of superimposition (the *āropya*)—being the subject (*viṣayin*)—swallows up or internalizes another object, namely the locus of superimposition (*āropa-viṣaya*), it is *sādhyavasānā*. //11//
These two types of difference are to be understood as figurative and literal, respectively, due to similarity and another type of relation.
These two— consisting of superimposition (*āropa*) and identification (*adhyavasāna*)— have similarity as their cause, as seen in the cases of "The Vāhīka is an ox" and "This is an ox."

Regarding this, some maintain that qualities such as dullness and slowness, which accompany the primary meaning (*svārtha*), even while being indicated (*lakṣyamāṇa*), serve as the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word "cow" when it denotes another object (*parārtha*).

Others hold that, through identity with the qualities accompanying the primary meaning, only the qualities inherent in the referent (*padārthagata*) are indicated, and the other object is not denoted by direct expression (*abhidhīyate*).
Others maintain that, by virtue of being the locus of common qualities, it is indicated solely for the sake of another;
and it has been stated elsewhere:
"Indication (lakṣaṇā) is defined as the cognition of something invariably concomitant with the primary meaning."
"However, figurative usage (gauṇatā) is accepted as arising from the connection with qualities perceived [in the primary object].
(Kumārila, *Tantravārttika* 3.4.12).
Here, "inseparable relation" (*avinābhāva*) refers to mere connection (*saṃbandhamātra*), and not to necessary concomitance (*nāntarīyakatva*).
For in reality, in cases such as "the beds cry out," there would be no indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Furthermore, it has been stated that since [the meaning] is established through implication (*ākṣepa*) alone when there is an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), indication serves no purpose.
And in cases such as "clarified butter is life" or "this is indeed life," there is another relation—such as cause and effect—that is distinct from similarity (*sādṛśya*).
In such cases, there is first an imposition (*āropa*) and then a determination (*adhyavasāya*) based on characteristics such as the relation of cause and effect.

Here, although there is a distinction between the two types of metaphorical (*gauṇa*) [superimposition], the purpose is the cognition of identity (*tādrūpyapratīti*) and the complete understanding of non-difference. However, in the case of the two pure (*śuddha*) [types of superimposition], the purpose is the capacity for causal efficacy and so forth, characterized by differentiation from others and by invariable concomitance (*avyabhicāra*).

In some cases, there is a metaphorical designation based on being for the sake of that [object], as when a pillar intended for Indra is called "Indra. In other cases, it is due to the relationship between owner and owned.
Just as a royal official is called "the king" in some cases due to the relationship between part and whole;
for example, in the expression "the tip of the hand," the term "hand" refers to the mere part that is the tip.
In some cases, it is due to performing that activity,
as for example, one who is not a carpenter is called a "carpenter."
...therefore, figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is of six kinds. // MK 12 //
Together with the first two divisions. //12//
And that [conventional meaning] is devoid of the suggested sense in the case of conventional usage, but it is accompanied by it in the case of a specific purpose;
for a specific purpose is indeed accessible only through the operation of suggestion.
And that [suggestion] may be either hidden or unhidden;
"that" refers to the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*). An example of the hidden is as follows:
Her face was blossoming with a smile; her glance possessed a captivating curvature; her gait was surging with amorous playfulness; her mind had cast aside all restraint;
her chest was adorned by budding breasts; and her hips were prominent with the curve of her shoulders.
In her body, which has eyes like lotus petals, the emergence of youth rejoices.
(Abhinavagupta’s *Dhvanyālokalocana*) An example of the unhidden (*agūḍha*) [suggestion] is as follows:
Through association with the wise, even the dull-witted become conversant with the conduct of the clever;
indeed, it is the intoxication of youth itself that teaches amorous women their graceful charms.
(Vallabhadeva’s *Subhāṣitāvali*)
He teaches this here.
... thus, this [emptiness] is said to be threefold. // MKpr-K_13 //

It is [also] that in which the suggested meaning is not subordinate (*avyaṅgyā*), that in which the suggested meaning is concealed (*gūḍhavyaṅgyā*), and that in which the suggested meaning is unconcealed (*agūḍhavyaṅgyā*). //13//
The word "tadbhūḥ" is connected with "the word is Lākṣaṇika"; "tadbhūḥ" means that which has that [primary meaning] as its basis.
In that case, the operation consists of suggestion (*vyañjanā*).
Why? He says:
"Because [suggestion] is resorted to in order to bring about the cognition of that [which is not directly expressed]. (MKV 14)
In this case, where the fruit (the meaning) is accessible solely through the word, there is no function other than suggestion (*vyañjanā*).
Where a word is employed through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with the desire to convey a specific purpose, the comprehension of that purpose does not arise from anything else, but from that very word;
and in such a case, there is no operation other than suggestion.
For instance,
there is no primary denotation because of the absence of convention;

in cases such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," those qualities such as purity which are perceived in the bank and so forth are not the meanings for which words like "Gaṅgā" have been conventionally established.
Because there is no logical reason, there is no figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).
The triad beginning with the sublation of the primary meaning is the cause. //15//
And thus, the indicated object is not primary; nor is there here a sublation [of the literal sense], nor is there a connection with a result;
there is no purpose in this, nor is the word's application faltering.

Just as the word "Ganges," being obstructed in its primary sense of the river current, indicates the bank, so too, if it were obstructed on the bank as well, it would indicate a further purpose. However, the bank is not the primary meaning here,
nor is there any obstruction in this context.
Furthermore, there is no connection between the bank—the referent of the word "Gaṅgā"—and the qualities such as sanctity that are to be indicated;
nor is there any purpose in the purpose itself being indicated;
nor is the word "Gaṅgā" incapable of conveying the purpose, just as it conveys the bank. (16)
Even so, there would be an infinite regress that destroys the very root.

If, even in this way, a purpose is perceived, it must be by means of another purpose, and that [other] purpose by yet another; thus, by failing to establish the subject at hand, an infinite regress would result.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the bank itself is indicated as being endowed with qualities such as sanctity, and that the purpose (*prayojana*) is the cognition of a meaning exceeding [the literal sense], as in "The hamlet is on the bank of the Gaṅgā"? Thus, since the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) applies to the qualified [object], why is there a need for suggestion (*vyañjanā*)? [Reply: It is said:
"It is not tenable for the indicated object to be accompanied by the purpose. (MK 17)
Why is this so? He says:
"For the object of cognition is one thing, while the fruit is said to be another.
In the case of perception and the like, blue and so forth are the object, whereas the fruit is either manifestation or consciousness."
There is no such indication (lakṣaṇā) for a qualified [object];
thus it has been explained.
... there would be specific distinctions in that which is characterized. // MK 18 //

The specific qualities such as sanctity and so forth, which reside in the riverbank and other such objects, are to be understood through a function distinct from denotation (*abhidhā*), intentionality (*tātparya*), and indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
And that function, expressed by terms such as *vyañjanā*, *dhvanana*, and *dyotana*, must necessarily be accepted. //18//
Thus, suggestiveness based on the literal meaning has been explained.

Regarding the basis of denotation, he says: "When the denotative capacity of a word with multiple meanings is restricted by [contextual factors] such as association (saṃyoga) and so forth, the function that produces the cognition of a non-denoted meaning is 'coloration' (añjana). (MK 19)
Association, dissociation, co-occurrence, opposition,
purpose, context, a characteristic mark, and the proximity of another word [are the factors that determine meaning].
Capacity, propriety, place, time, gender, accent, and so forth,
are the causes for the recollection of specific meanings when the meaning of a word is otherwise undetermined.
(Bhartṛhari, Vākyapadīya 2.315–316)
According to the direction thus stated,
Hari, who possesses the conch and discus, is called "Hari without the conch and discus"; likewise,
[the names] Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa are used for the son of Daśaratha.
"Rāmārjunagatiḥ tayor" refers to Bhārgava and Kārtavīrya;
"Sthāṇuṃ bhaja bhavacchide" refers to Hara;
and "Sarvaṃ jānāti devaḥ" refers to Your Majesty.
"Enraged Makaradhvaja" refers to Kāma;
"of the god who is the enemy of Pura" refers to Śambhu;
"the cuckoo intoxicated by honey" refers to Spring.
"May your beloved’s face protect you" is used when there is mutual presence (*sāṃmukhya*).

"The Supreme Lord shines here" is used with respect to the king, by way of the region in the form of the capital. "The sun shines" is used with respect to the sun during the day, and with respect to fire at night.
In the case of *mitraṃ bhāti* ("the friend shines") when referring to a well-wisher, and *mitro bhāti* ("the sun shines"),
as well as in Vedic examples such as *indraśatruḥ* ("having Indra as his enemy"), it is only in the Veda— and not in poetry— that accentuation produces a specific understanding [of meaning].
This is because of the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*).

With breasts of such a size, with eyelashes of such a length, in such a state, and in so many days. (11) [She has breasts of this very measure, with eyelashes of this very measure; she is in this very condition, after this many days.]

Because there is no determination regarding the specific nature of the relationship— whether "these belong only to the neutral observer," or "these belong only to me," or "these belong only to the enemy," or "these belong only to the neutral observer"—

the stable emotion (*sthāyin*), such as love (*rati*) and so forth, which exists as a latent impression (*vāsanā*) within the spectators, is manifested through these [objects] perceived in a universal manner.

Like the juice of a beverage being savored, appearing as if right before one's eyes, entering as if into the heart, embracing all the limbs, obscuring everything else, and evoking an experience like the tasting of Brahman— the *rasa* such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and others produces a transcendental wonder.

(Kālidāsa’s *Vikramorvaśīya* 4.4) Here, there is a complex intermingling (*śabalatā*) of deliberation, longing, intelligence, recollection, apprehension, dejection, fortitude, and anxiety; thus, the state of the transitory emotions (*bhāva*) has been both described and illustrated. //36//

Even when they are in the primary rasa, those— namely the *bhāva-śānti* (subsidence of emotion) and so forth— sometimes attain the status of the dominant (*aṅgin*). This status of being the dominant is like that of a servant engaged in a marriage procession following a king.
But that which exists as a suggested meaning whose sequence is perceptible, appearing like an after-sound (anusvāna); // 37 //
That *dhvani* is said to be threefold, arising from the power of both word and meaning:
that which has as its suggested content (*vyaṅgya*) a resonance (*anuraṇana*) rooted in the power of the word,
and that which has as its suggested content a resonance rooted in the power of the meaning.
And that which consists of a suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) in the form of a resonance based on both powers; thus, it is threefold. //37//
In that regard,
there is [the figure of] ornament (alaṅkāra) and also the thing itself (vastu), where either the word or other [elements] appear.
That [suggested meaning] arising from the power of the word (*śabdaśaktyudbhava*) is to be known as twofold by virtue of its predominance:
the "thing" (*vastu*) and the "non-ornament" (*analaṅkāra*), which is the mere thing itself. An example of the former is:
"Having raised the great cloud of the black sword..."
By that King, with his aged yet powerful thundering,
the entire blazing majesty of his enemies in battle was extinguished throughout the three worlds by the waters of his [sword’s] edge. (54)

(Śivasvāmin’s *Kapphiṇābhyudaya* 1.24) Here, lest the sentence be charged with expressing an incoherent meaning, one must conceive of a relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) between the contextual and the non-contextual; thus, the figure of speech *upamā* (simile) is suggested (*vyaṅgya*). [The verse continues:
"O Lord, you who possess the heat of fierce rays, yet create the night for the moon, and whose play is sweet..."
"O wise one, you shine as one whose conduct accords with reality and who is the leader of both sides at every step.
(Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*) Here, by taking each individual word as a compound of two words, there arises the figure of speech known as *virodhābhāsa* (the semblance of contradiction).
O Lord, you are immeasurable through the excellences attained by those who have reached you; you grant joy;
and you are unfriendly to the wicked, yet united with the fame of the virtuous.
(56) (Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*)
Here too, there is an apparent contradiction:
"Homage to that wielder of the trident, who, praiseworthy for his artistic skill, unfolds the variegated world-picture upon a wall-less surface, without any accumulation of material causes. (57)
In this [verse], there is the figure of speech *vyatireka* (distinction).
Even though it is the object to be embellished (*alaṅkārya*), it functions as an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) according to the maxim of the "Brahmin and the ascetic" (*brāhmaṇa-śramaṇa*).
"O traveler, there is no bedding here in this village of stony ground; if you wish to stay after seeing the high and low terrain, then stay. (58)
"O traveler, there is not even the slightest straw-mat here in this village of rocky ground;
if you can sleep embracing a high-breasted woman, then stay.
(Hāla’s *Gāthāsaptaśatī* 879)
In this context, it is implied: "If you are capable of enjoying [this], then sit here.
"O King, he upon whom you are wrathful is struck down violently by both thunderbolt and lightning;
yet he with whom you are pleased shines forth, both noble and magnificent. (59)
(Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*) It is suggested that even though they are not in opposition, they perform a single action for the sake of following you.
Furthermore, the meaning arising from the power of the sense (*arthaśaktyudbhava*) is a suggester (*vyañjaka*) when it is possible by its own nature (*svataḥ*).
Whether established through mere bold assertion by the poet or by what is fashioned by him,
this [suggestion], which has six varieties— consisting of either a fact or an ornament— manifests that [meaning].
Alternatively, it may be a matter of fact (*vastu*) or an ornament (*alaṅkāra*); thus, this [suggested meaning] consists of twelve types.
It is not merely produced by being spoken; rather, it is that which is possible even in the external world through propriety (*aucitya*).

Furthermore, there are two other kinds: that which is created by the poet’s mere imagination even if it does not exist externally, and that which is uttered by a character created by the poet. Thus, it is threefold.
Whether it be a fact (*vastu*) or an ornament (*alaṅkāra*), that [suggestive word] is of six kinds as a suggester (*vyañjaka*).

Since its suggested content (*vyaṅgya*) is either a fact or an ornament, there are twelve varieties of *dhvani* arising from the power of meaning (*arthaśaktyudbhava*). The examples follow in order: 1. *Vastu-vyañjaka* (suggesting a fact): *mugdhe mugdhatayaiva netum akhilaḥ kālaḥ kim ārabhyate* "O innocent one, why do you begin to spend all your time in such innocence? 2. *Alaṅkāra-vyañjaka* (suggesting an ornament): *khaṃ vaste kalavāgminī sthagayati svaṃ locanadvandvakaṃ* "The sweet-voiced [night] wears the sky [as a garment]; she covers her own pair of eyes... 3. *Vastu-vyaṅgya* (a fact suggested by a fact): *unnidrakokanadareṇupiśaṅgitāṅgā* "Her limbs are reddened by the pollen of full-blown red lotuses... 4. *Alaṅkāra-vyaṅgya* (an ornament suggested by a fact): *gacchāmy acyuta darśanena bhavataḥ kiṃ tṛptirutpadyate* "I am going, O Acyuta; can satisfaction ever arise from merely seeing you? 5. *Vastu-vyaṅgya* (a fact suggested by an ornament): *subhage koṭir eṣā na gaṇyate* "O fortunate one, this is not even counted as a crore... 6. *Alaṅkāra-vyaṅgya* (an ornament suggested by an ornament): *kassa va ṇa hoi roso daṭṭhūṇa piāi savvaṇaṃ aharam* "Who would not feel resentment upon seeing the bitten lip of his beloved? Thus, there are twelve types of *dhvani* arising from the power of meaning. Examples follow in sequence.
"The crown jewel of the indolent, the foremost among rogues, O daughter, filled with an abundance of wealth"— upon hearing these words, Nāgaṅgī’s eyes blossomed wide with joy. (60)
Thus, upon these words being spoken, the lady of curved limbs became one whose eyes blossomed wide.
(Hāla’s *Gāthāsaptaśatī* 970).
Here, by means of the fact (*vastu*) that "she is to be enjoyed by me alone," another fact is suggested (*vyañjaka*).
Blessed are you, who can utter hundreds of confident and playful endearments even during the intervals of lovemaking with your beloved;
yet when your lover places his hand upon the knot of your lower garment—
"Friends, I swear that I do not remember even the slightest [fault].
(Śārṅgadharapaddhati).
Here, the figure of speech is *vyatireka* (contrast), in which she implies: "In this matter, you are unfortunate, whereas I am fortunate."

In battle, the heroes beheld his splendor, crimson with thick blood flowing from the frontal globes of scent-elephants blinded by pride, as he appeared with a countenance darkened by the wrath of anger.
"In whose hand the sword is like the sidelong glance of Kālī.
(Śivasvāmin’s *Kapphiṇābhyudaya* 1.37).
Here, by means of the poetic figure of simile (*upamā*), the fact (*vastu*) that the destruction of the entire enemy force will be accomplished in an instant is suggested.
He who, in battle, out of rage bit his own lower lip, thereby releasing the coral-like lips of the wives of his enemies from the perilous pain of the deep tooth-wounds inflicted by their beloveds.
(Viśvanātha’s *Sāhityadarpaṇa* 4.9)

Here, through the figure of contradiction (*virodhālaṅkāra*), it is suggested by the figure of parallelism (*tulyayogitā*) that the enemies were destroyed at the very moment the lower lip was bitten; furthermore, the thought "May the injury of another be averted even by my own injury" is poetically imagined—thus there is also the figure of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). In these examples, the suggestor (*vyañjaka*) is inherently possible (*svataḥsaṃbhavī*).
On the first peak of Kailāsa, having heard his fame being sung by the beloved goddesses of the gods with the melodies of the flute, the deer—
casting their sidelong glances and suspecting them to be the stalks of lotus plants growing in a lake— [flee].
"The elephants of the quarters wave their trunks upon the sandy banks of their ears.

(Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*) Here, by means of the expressed fact (*vastu*), the suggested fact (*vastu-dhvani*) is conveyed: "Your fame produces such a wonder even in those who possess no understanding of meaning, by generating such perceptions in them."
By him, the glory of victory was seized by force by the hair in battle, so that his enemies were firmly established within his throat, as if in mountain caves.
"Just as the caves, distressed by him, firmly clung to his neck"—
in this [verse from Hāla’s *Gāthāsaptaśatī* 971],
there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that the caves, as if their passion were inflamed by the sight of him seizing her hair, grasp those who are separated from him by the throat.

Because victory is seen in a single battle, his enemies flee and remain in caves; this is the poetic figure *kāvyahetu* (poetic cause). Furthermore, it is not that his enemies have fled, but rather that the caves do not abandon them out of apprehension of defeat from him; this is the figure *apahnuti* (concealment).
[In the Prakrit verse: "O lover, quickly descend upon this mountain cave, which is a secret place for a firm embrace."
When her lover is eager for a firm embrace, the pride of the high-minded woman quickly retreats from her heart, as if afraid of being crushed.

Victorious is that speech which, as if laughing at the Elder [the Veda], having taken its seat upon the lotus-face of the poet, reveals the circle of the world as if it were something else entirely. //67//

(Hāla’s *Gāthāsaptaśatī* 982) Here, through poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), which is the sole cause of aesthetic wonder, there is the figure of contrast (*vyatireka*) that she, seated upon a non-insentient throne, creates a world ever-new and ever-new.
In these cases, the suggester (*vyañjaka*) is produced solely by the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of the poet.

Those Malaya breezes, which once attained poverty by being swallowed by the rows of hoods— puffed out in anger at the heavy sighs of the hips of women exhausted by amorous play upon the slopes of Mount Laṅkā— now come into contact with the sighs of women separated from their lovers.
Those [lotuses] which, though thick even in their childhood, have suddenly become full of youth—
[those lotuses] which, having slipped away from the slopes of Mount Laṅkā while being swallowed by the wide-open rows of hoods of female serpents exhausted by amorous play, have fallen into poverty.
Now these Malaya breezes, having come into contact with the sighs of women separated from their lovers,
have suddenly become thick— though still in their infancy— as if they were already full of youth.

In this passage, by means of the fact that "the winds, having attained sovereignty through [her] sighs, do what they will," one thing suggests another thing (*vastunā vastu vyajyate*). "O friend, having overcome my pride through fortitude, I had regained hope; yet suddenly, by him whose nature is fickle in the matter of seeing his beloved, that hope was cast down. (69)
"O friend, having created a semblance of composure for my pride, he suddenly departed at the very moment my heart was rendered helpless by the sight of my beloved. (Hāla’s *Gāthāsaptaśatī* 936)

In this case, even though no request has been made, she is gracious; thus there is the figure of speech *vibhāvanā*. Alternatively, there is the figure of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), suggesting that the power of the beloved’s beauty cannot be endured by her fortitude.
{With eyes whose pupils are moist with tears, I have bestowed a red garment upon your eyes as a favor; yet these [eyes] have not been stepped upon by anger.} (70)
A red garment was given by you to my two eyes with fresh wounds from your fingernails and teeth;
yet, in anger, these [eyes] have not returned the favor.
(Hāla’s *Gāthāsaptaśatī* 971)

In this verse, by means of the figure of speech *uttarālaṅkāra* (the answer), the following fact (*vastu*) is suggested: "Why do you bear such angry eyes?"—it is not merely that you conceal the fresh nail-marks, but rather that I have become the recipient of your favor.
{O happy one, she who fills your heart with a thousand women, though unable to endure it, day after day performs no other task but makes her already slender body even more emaciated. //71//}
O fortunate one, she, finding no room within your heart already filled with thousands of women,
day after day— devoted to no other task— makes even her slender body grow thinner.
(Hāla’s *Gāthāsaptaśatī* 2.82)

Here, by means of the figure of speech *hetu* (causation), there is the figure of speech *viśeṣokti* (exceptional statement), which asserts that even though her body has been made thin, [the pain] does not reside in your heart.
In these cases, the suggester has its form established solely through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of a speaker fashioned by the poet.
Thus, there are twelve varieties.
The one who consists of both word and meaning...

Now, one might ask: since the *rasas* and so forth possess many subdivisions, how can there be eighteen? To this, he says:
"Because the *rasas* and so forth are infinite, their variety is counted as one.
Regarding the phrase "because they are infinite": [it means that] because they are infinite.
For instance: there are nine rasas.
Among them, there are two divisions of śṛṅgāra:
saṃbhoga and vipralambha.

Even within *saṃbhoga* (union), there are many varieties, such as mutual gazing, embracing, kissing, gathering flowers, sporting in water, and descriptions of the sunset, moonrise, and the six seasons.
For *vipralambha* (separation), longing and so forth have been mentioned;
yet both of these possess a manifold variety of determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory mental states (*vyabhicāribhāva*).
Even therein, there are superior, middling, and inferior natures for the two protagonists;
and even within those, there are distinctions of place, time, situation, and so forth—thus, there is an infinity of a single rasa alone. What need is there to mention others?
However, by relying on the commonality of being sequential (kramatva), the various types of suggestion such as rasa and so forth are counted as a single category.
In a sentence, there is that which arises from both...
"arising from both" means it is rooted in the power of both word and meaning.
"...others [hold that it occurs] even in a single word (*pade 'pyanye*).
By the word "even" (*api*), it is implied that it occurs in a sentence as well.

Just as a beautiful woman shines by means of an ornament placed on a single limb, so too does speech (*bhāratī*) shine when the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), though residing in a single word, illuminates the entire sentence.
In that regard, here are examples illustrating manifestation through words (*padaprakāśyatva*) in successive order:
"He whose friends are [truly] friends and whose enemies are [truly] enemies, and who is compassionate toward those worthy of compassion—he is truly born, and he truly lives. (73) (1)

when her friend had thus exhorted her, she, with a frightened face, spoke this reply to her:

Since there is no greater aesthetic charm (*vaicitrya*) when states of being (*bhāva*) and so forth are manifested by words, they are not illustrated here.
[His] staff-like arms, beautiful and formidable with swords adorned by streams of blood...

It has been stated here that the fruits of evil deeds and good deeds, which would otherwise have to be experienced over thousands of births, are experienced through the sorrow of separation and the joy of reflection [respectively].
Thus, there is a hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) illuminated by the words *aśeṣa* (entire) and *caya* (accumulation). [The night] was not a night; the forest was not a forest; calamity was not a calamity.
"Alas, O hero! When you turn your back upon your enemies, everything turns its back.

(Subhāṣitaratnabhāṇḍāgāra 103/74) Here, by means of the *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration) based on the *virodhāṅga* (apparent contradiction) rooted in the power of the words (*śabdaśaktimūla*), the suggested matter (*vastu*)—"Even the Creator follows you"—is illuminated by the word "everything" (*sarva*).
"In the morning, your beloved’s lower lip was like a withered lotus petal"; having heard this, the young bride speaks these words directly to the bull. (83) (9)

As for the suggested meaning of the relationship (*saṃbandha*): [it is illustrated by the example: "The king’s servant. Here, the word "king" suggests that he is a man of great power and majesty; the word "servant" suggests that he is one who has attained the highest degree of excellence through his devotion to his master. Furthermore, the relationship between them—namely, that of master and servant—is such that it suggests the servant is one who has been thoroughly tested and found trustworthy. This is because, in the absence of such a relationship, the servant would not be able to carry out the king's commands with such confidence. Thus, the relationship itself conveys a specific excellence. Similarly, in the phrase "The king’s mountain," the word "king" suggests that the mountain is vast, while the word "mountain" suggests that the king is a sovereign whose dominion extends over the entire earth. Moreover, the relationship between them—namely, that of possessor and possessed—is such that it suggests the mountain is a source of jewels and other treasures, and the king is one who possesses the power to protect all beings. This is because, in the absence of such a relationship, the mountain would not be a source of jewels, nor would the king be a protector. Thus, the relationship itself conveys a specific excellence. Likewise, in the phrase "The Brahmin’s staff," the word "Brahmin" suggests that the staff is made of *vaṃśa* wood, while the word "staff" suggests that the Brahmin is one who is well-versed in the Vedas and the like. Furthermore, the relationship between them—namely, that of owner and owned—is such that it suggests the staff is free from wear and tear, and the Brahmin is one who is pure in conduct. This is because, in the absence of such a relationship, the staff would not be free from wear and tear, nor would the Brahmin be pure in conduct. Thus, the relationship itself conveys a specific excellence. Similarly, in the phrase "The cowherd’s daughter," the word "cowherd" suggests that she is beautiful, while the word "daughter" suggests that she is one who is skilled in the arts of love. Furthermore, the relationship between them—namely, that of father and daughter—is such that it suggests the cowherd is one who is devoted to his own wife, and the daughter is one who is modest. This is because, in the absence of such a relationship, the cowherd would not be devoted to his own wife, nor would the daughter be modest. Thus, the relationship itself conveys a specific excellence. Likewise, in the phrase "The king’s elephant," the word "king" suggests that the elephant is large in size, while the word "elephant" suggests that the king is one who is skilled in the art of warfare. Furthermore, the relationship between them—namely, that of master and mount—is such that it suggests the elephant is swift in its gait and the king is one who is capable of conquering his enemies. Thus, the relationship itself conveys a specific excellence. Similarly, in the phrase "The Brahmin’s son," the word "Brahmin" suggests that the son is well-behaved, while the word "son" suggests that the Brahmin is one who is intent on performing sacrifices and the like. Thus, the relationship itself conveys a specific excellence. In this way, the suggested meanings arising from words, meanings, and relationships are infinite.
