Here, the Śiva, the destroyer of Smara, is simultaneously assailed by haste and languor;
this is a *saṃdhi* (juncture) between agitation (*āvega*) and fortitude (*dhairya*).
"Look! O fickle one, O restless one, what haste is this? I am but a young maiden; give me a hand to hold! Alas, alas! What a transgression—where are you going?
Thus did the daughter of the forest-dweller, the enemy of you, O Lord of the Earth, speak.
A certain maiden, gathering fruits and sprouts, says [this].
(Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*) Herein, there is a blending (*śabalatā*) of apprehension, envy, fortitude, memory, fatigue, dejection, awakening, and eagerness.
And these are the *alaṃkāras* such as *rasavat* and so forth.

Although the emergence of emotion (*bhāvodaya*), the conjunction of emotions (*bhāvasaṃdhi*), and the commingling of emotions (*bhāvaśabalatva*) have not been mentioned as *alaṃkāras*, they are mentioned here in case someone might say so.

Furthermore, although there is no subject matter where a mixture (*saṃkara*) or a combination (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of *dhvani* and *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*—along with their own respective subdivisions and so on—does not exist, nevertheless, designations are made according to what is predominant.
Thus, in some cases, there is conventional usage based on something by someone:
"In Janasthāna, with my mind blinded by the golden mirage, I wandered;
at every step, I uttered tearful lamentations, crying out 'Vaidehī!'"
I have performed the composition of arrows for the face of the Lord of Alakā;
I have attained the state of Rāma, yet I have not achieved the status of being the son of Kuśa and Lava.
(Śrīvatsalāñchanācārya’s *Kāvyaparīkṣā* 66)

Here, the simile consisting of a suggested resonance (*anuraṇana*) based on the power of the word— the relationship of object of comparison and subject of comparison with Rāma— is made subordinate to the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
"Having arrived, she whose limbs are now disordered by separation..."
Behold, O slender-limbed one, how the thousand-rayed sun, having spent the three watches of the night elsewhere, now slowly propitiates this lotus pond at dawn by falling at her feet. (125) (2)

(Śrīvatsalāñchanācārya’s *Kāvyaparīkṣā* 67) Here, the narrative of the hero— which is based on the power of the literal meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*) and takes the form of a factual matter (*vastu*)— subsists solely through the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of the narrative of the sun and the lotus, which is independent [of that hero].
An example of that which is subordinate to the accomplishment of the expressed meaning (*vācyasiddhyaṅga*) is as follows:

"Poison produced by the serpent-cloud forcibly brings about whirling, restlessness, dejection of heart, dissolution, fainting, darkness, exhaustion of the body, and death for women separated from their lovers. (126)
(Ānandavardhana’s *Dhvanyāloka* 2.3) Here, *hālāhala* is the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), which serves to establish the literal meaning (*vācya*) of the form of a serpent. Or, for example:
"I am going, O Acyuta; can satisfaction ever arise from merely seeing you?"
"Yet, while we two are thus alone, these wretched people imagine otherwise.
May Hari protect you—he whose body bristled with horripilation as he embraced the gopī, who was languid with the weariness of her futile stay, a state betrayed by the tone of that address. 127. (3)
In this case, the suggested meaning conveyed by words such as "Acyuta" is subordinate to the expressed meaning, such as the act of addressing.
Furthermore, the distinction between these two lies in the fact that in one instance they reside in a single speaker, whereas in the other they reside in different speakers.
It is indistinct, as in:
"When you are unseen, there is longing to see you; when seen, there is fear of separation.
Neither by being unseen nor by being seen is happiness obtained from you. (128) (4)
(Govindaṭhakkura’s Kāvyapradīpa) Here,
[the expression] "act in such a way that you are not seen and that the fear of separation does not arise" is considered *kliṣṭa* (obscure).
An example of that where the predominance is doubtful is as follows:
"But Hara, his composure slightly shaken like the ocean at the onset of moonrise, cast his eyes upon Umā’s face, with its bimba-fruit-like lower lip. (129) (5)
In this verse from Kālidāsa’s *Kumārasambhava* (3.67),
there is a doubt as to whether the implied sense— that she desired to kiss him— is primary, or whether the literal expression— the movement of the eyes— is primary.
An example of equal prominence:
"The abandonment of the offense against the Brahmins is for your very welfare; thus Jāmadagnya is your friend, otherwise he would be displeased. (130)
In this passage from Bhavabhūti’s *Mahāvīracarita* (2.8),

the suggested meaning— that the son of Jamadagni will, in an instant, bring about the destruction of all the Rākṣasas as he did of all the Kṣatriyas— and the expressed meaning possess equal prominence.
An example of what is suggested by intonation (*kākvākṣipta*) is as follows:
"Shall I not, out of wrath, crush a hundred Kauravas in battle?
Shall I not drink the blood of Duḥśāsana from his chest?"
I shall crush Suyodhana’s thighs with my mace;
let the king make peace with you on the condition of a wager.
(1.15) (Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa’s *Veṇīsaṃhāra*)
In this case, the suggested meaning, beginning with "I indeed churn," exists simultaneously with the negation of the literal expression.
An example of the unpleasant:
"The limbs of the young woman, busy with household chores, are chilled as she listens to the clamor of the swallows flying up from the thicket of reeds. (132) (8)
The limbs of the young wife, occupied with household chores, grow weary as she hears the clamor of birds taking flight from the thicket of *vānīra* reeds. (Hāla’s *Gāthāsaptaśatī* 876)

In this case, because of the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) that "someone who has received a secret signal has entered the thicket of creepers," the expressed meaning (vācya), "my limbs are languishing," becomes endowed with aesthetic charm (sacamatkāra).
Their subdivisions should be understood, as appropriate, to be as previously described.
"According to the circumstances":
"When figures of speech are manifested by the mere thing itself,
then they certainly constitute a part of suggestion (dhvani), because poetic function depends upon them."

Thus, according to the direction stated by the author of the *Dhvanyāloka*, where a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is manifested by a mere matter (*vastumātra*), there is no status of "subordinated suggestion" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*). "With those [figures] accompanied by figures" means: with those very figures, and with those [matters] joined with figures; [this occurs] through their conjunction (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) or commingling (*saṅkara*) with *dhvani*.
As it has been stated by the author of the Dhvanyāloka:

"That [Suggestive Poetry] shines forth in many ways, together with its own subdivisions— those in which the suggested meaning is subordinate (guṇībhūtavyaṅgya) and those accompanied by figures of speech (sālaṅkāra)— and furthermore, through the combinations of commingling (saṃkara) and coexistence (saṃsṛṣṭi)."
Thus,
through their mutual conjunction alone, the number of divisions would become exceedingly great.
In this manner, by counting the intermediate subdivisions, the enumeration becomes exceedingly vast;
for indeed, in the enumeration of the divisions and subdivisions of even a single horn, there is infinity—
what need is there to mention the enumeration of them all?
Furthermore, when summarized, this *dhvani* has three varieties, because the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) possesses three forms. To explain:
some [suggested meanings] tolerate being expressed (*vācyatā*), while others do not.

In this regard, that which is capable of being expressed is both non-variegated (*avicitra*) and variegated (*vicitra*). The non-variegated is the mere object (*vastumātra*), while the variegated consists of the form of poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
Although the latter is primarily the object to be adorned (*alaṅkārya*), it is nevertheless so designated according to the maxim of the "Brahmin and the ascetic" (*brāhmaṇa-śramaṇa-nyāya*).
However, an object characterized as rasa and so forth cannot be denoted even in a dream;
for it would have to be expressed either by the word "rasa" or by words such as "śṛṅgāra.

Yet it is not so expressed, because even when those [words] are employed, it is not apprehended if the *vibhāvas* and so forth are not employed, and conversely, it is apprehended even when they are not employed.

Because it is apprehended through the employment of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, as established by both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is determined that it is perceived solely by means of the denotation of the excitants and so on;
therefore, it is indeed *vyaṅgya* (suggestible).
Because there is no sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*) and so forth, it is not to be indicated (*lakṣaṇīya*) again.

It was established previously that in the cases of "transferred" (*saṃkramita*) and "entirely set aside" (*atyantatiraskṛta*) denotable meanings, indication itself would not even occur without a suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*) in the form of a mere fact (*vastumātra*).

However, in the case of [suggestion] rooted in the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*), since the primary function of denotation (*abhidhā*) is restricted, the status of another meaning—which is not directly denoted—as a suggestion, along with figures of speech such as simile (*upamā*) and the like, is beyond dispute.

Even in the case of that [theory] based on the power of meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*), it is not tenable to establish a convention (*saṃketa*) regarding a specific [particular], because words have objects in the form of universals (*sāmānyarūpa*). Therefore, in the theory of "the connection of what has been expressed" (*abhihitānvayavāda*), where the sentence-meaning is a specific form— even though it is not itself a word-meaning— the mutual connection of word-meanings occurs by virtue of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*saṃnidhi*), and compatibility (*yogyatā*).
What then is the status of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) if it were to be the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*)?
Regarding this, they also say:
"In this case, one perceives by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) the words, the elders, and the objects denoted."
And the listener's state of having understood [the meaning] is established through inference based on their physical activity. //1//

But by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), based on the impossibility of [the word's function] otherwise, one should understand the twofold power of cognition; thus, the relationship is known through three means of valid cognition.
(2) [Kumārilabhaṭṭa]

In the manner thus established, when an elder (the "superior") utters a sentence such as "Devadatta, bring the cow," and the intermediate elder (the "middle-aged") leads the object possessing a dewlap and other features to another location, [the child] infers through that action that "this person has understood such a meaning from this very sentence.
Thereby, by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), he perceives the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācya-vācaka-bhāva*) between that indivisible sentence and its sentence-meaning.
Having ascertained the relationship [between word and meaning], the child becomes proficient therein.

When sentences such as "Caitra, bring the cow," "Devadatta, bring the horse," or "Devadatta, lead the cow" are employed by others, he ascertains the respective meaning of each individual word through the methods of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Thus, it is the sentence alone that effects engagement and withdrawal.

Regarding the phrase "suitable for application" (*prayogayogyam*), the convention (*saṃketa*) is grasped precisely as that of words situated within a sentence, which are already related to their respective word-meanings (*padārtha*).
Thus, the sentence-meanings (*vākyārtha*) are indeed the qualified word-meanings themselves;
it is not, however, a qualification *of* the word-meanings.

Although it is determined by the cognition of recognition that these very same words are those employed in other sentences— and thus the word-meaning is the object of convention as being related merely to another word-meaning— nevertheless, according to the proponents of the theory of "expression of the related" (anvitābhidhāna), that meaning is understood precisely in its specific form as delimited by a universal, because word-meanings are of such a nature when they are interconnected.

Even in their view, the referent of a word (*padārtha*)—being of the nature of a universal-particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*)—is the object of linguistic convention (*saṃketa*). However, that which is the ultimate particular (*ativiśeṣa*), being included within the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), is strictly unexpressible because it is not the object of convention. Where such a word-referent is understood, there is no question at all of another meaning, such as a command (*vidhi*) and so forth, in cases like "niḥśeṣacyuta... and the like. In the theory of "expression of the related" (*abhihitānvaya*), the meaning is unrelated [to other words] by itself; in the theory of "expression of the related" (*anvitābhidhāna*), it is related merely to other word-meanings. But the specific related meaning (*anvitaviśeṣa*) is indeed unexpressible. Thus, in both systems, the sentence-meaning is strictly not a word-referent (*apadārtha*).
As for the claim that signs are postulated in accordance with their effects (*naimittika*),
in that case, the status of being a sign (*nimittatva*) for a word must be either its capacity as a producer (*kārakatva*) or its capacity as an indicator (*jñāpakatva*).
Since it is an illuminator (*prakāśaka*), it does not possess the capacity of a producer.
But how can there be the status of being an indicator (*jñāpakatva*) for that which is unknown?

And its knownness occurs only through convention (*saṃketa*); and since that [convention] applies only to what is accompanied by a relation (*anvita*), as long as the fixed nature of the cause (*nimitta*) is not ascertained, how can there even be the cognition of the effect (*naimittika*)? Thus, "the causes are postulated in accordance with the effects."
This is an unexamined assertion.

As for those who maintain that "this is a single operation, like that of an arrow, which becomes increasingly longer and longer," and that "the meaning of a word is that toward which the word is directed," and thus that "only the injunction (vidhi) is the expressed meaning here"—
they too are ignorant of the intended purport (tātparya), and their talk about purport is merely a way of speaking to please the gods.

For it is said: "In the utterance of what has already come to be, that which has come to be is taught for the sake of what is yet to be. Thus, the meanings of the case-words (kāraka-pada) attain the state of being something to be accomplished (sādhyamānatā) through their connection with action.
Consequently, according to the maxim of "burning what is not yet burned," only that which has not yet been attained is enjoined.
This is as when the performance of the officiating priests is already established by another means of knowledge (pramāṇa).

In the case of the statement, "The officiating priests proceed wearing red turbans," only the state of wearing a red turban is the thing to be enjoined, since the act of offering is already established from another source; likewise, in such cases as "He offers with curd," only the status of the curd as an instrument is the thing to be enjoined.

In some cases there is an injunction of two [factors], and in others even an injunction of three, as in "Weave a red cloth" (*raktaṃ paṭaṃ vaya*), where there may be an injunction of one, two, or three [elements].

Consequently, "the intention (*tātparya*) resides precisely in that which is to be enjoined"; thus, the intention lies in the meaning of the word actually employed, and not merely in what is understood. For otherwise, in such cases as "The one who was in front runs," the intention might sometimes reside in the "one who was behind" (*apara*) and so forth.

As for the claim that in the statement "Eat poison, but do not eat in another's house," the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is "One must not eat in this house," and therefore that alone is the sentence-meaning—it is replied: in that case, the word *ca* (and) serves to indicate syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*). Furthermore, there is no relationship of primary and subordinate between two verbal sentences; thus, one must assume that the sentence regarding eating poison is subordinate because it is the speech of a friend. [The implication is: "This house is more wicked than even eating poison."
In the case of "Do not eat in his house under any circumstances," the intention (tātparya) lies precisely in the meaning already grasped by the words.

If the function of denotation (abhidhā) of a word were limited only to that much of a meaning as is obtained immediately after hearing the word, then how [could one explain] the examples: "A son has been born to you, O Brāhmaṇa" and "Your daughter-in-law is pregnant, O Brāhmaṇa"?
In such cases, even joy, sorrow, and the like are not the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
Why? Because even regarding the indicated meaning (*lakṣaṇīya*), comprehension is established through a process of denotation (*abhidhā*) that is increasingly prolonged.

Furthermore, why is it that among direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*), each preceding one is stronger than the following? Thus, even within the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna-vāda*), the suggestiveness (*vyaṅgyatva*) of the injunction (*vidhi*) is established.
Furthermore, regarding the reversal of the two words "kiṃ ca" and "kuru rucim" within a poem, how could there be defectiveness?
For in this case, an indecent meaning is not connected with other word-meanings; thus, it would be non-denotable [and therefore not a defect]. Such instances would have to be left unexcluded.

Moreover, if the relationship between the suggested and the suggester (vyaṅgyavyañjakabhāva) were not accepted as distinct from the relationship between the expressed and the expresser (vācyavācakatva), then grammatical incorrectness (*asādhutva*) and the like would be permanent defects, while harshness (*kaṣṭatva*) and the like would be occasional defects.
The establishment of a distinction [between the two] would be untenable;
yet it is not untenable, because everything indeed appears as distinct.

However, if one resorts to the relationship between the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) rather than the relationship between the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*), then—given the manifold nature of the manifested—the systematic arrangement of the distinction is indeed possible, as it occurs appropriately in specific instances for specific [manifestors].

In such passages as, "The pair has now fallen into a state of lamentability through their longing for union with the Skull-bearer (Kapālin)," why is it that words such as *kapālin* are more conducive to poetry than words like *pinākin*? Furthermore, the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) is uniform toward all recipients of the communication; thus, it is fixed.
For in such cases as "the sun has set," the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) never varies;
however, the suggested meaning (*pratīyamāna*), by virtue of being assisted by specific factors such as the particular context, the speaker, and the listener, assumes manifold forms.
Thus, from the statement "the sun has set," one may understand, for instance, that this is the opportunity to launch a surprise attack against an enemy.

"Let us set out for the rendezvous," "Your beloved is almost here," "Let us cease from our work," "Let the evening rites be commenced," "Do not go far," "Let the cows be brought home," "There is no more heat now," "Let the goods for sale be gathered in," "The beloved has still not arrived"— such is the endless range of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
The meaning manifests itself in various places;

in the verse beginning with "niḥśeṣa" regarding speech and penance, it appears in the form of both prohibition and injunction: "O noble ones, casting aside envy and reflecting upon what must be done, let them speak with propriety."
In such passages as "Should one serve the hips of the mountains, or rather those of amorous, smiling women?
(Bhartṛhari’s *Śṛṅgāraśataka* 36), [the figure of speech is] in the form of a resolution situated within a state of doubt between the peaceful and the erotic sentiments.
O King, how can you feel pride that you have seized the fortune of your enemies whose heads were shattered by the edge of your sharp sword?
Surely, even after you had slain those foes, did she not already belong to you?
In such passages as "Their beloved fame has departed for the third heaven with their limbs" (from Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*), the nature [of the figure] consists of censure and praise.

Regarding the cause [of the distinction]: it is established by the perception of a temporal sequence (pūrvapaścādbhāva); regarding the substratum: it is established by the fact that time has sound as its locus, and that [the meaning] has as its locus the word, its parts, its referent, the phonemes, and their syntactic arrangement;

regarding the means of cognition: it is understood through the knowledge of grammar (*śabdānuśāsana*), aided by context (*prakaraṇa*) and the like, together with the clarity of intuition (*pratibhā*); and regarding the result: it consists of the designation of "mere cognizer" versus "erudite," and the aesthetic wonder (*camatkṛti*) arising from mere cognition.
From the effect [one infers] the cause, according to the method demonstrated in such cases as "The sun has set," and so forth; likewise, from number [one infers the cause]:
"Who indeed would not feel anger upon seeing his beloved’s bitten lip?
O you who are perverse in your refusal of water, now endure [the consequences] of having devoured the lotus along with the bees! (135)
"Or who would not feel anger upon seeing the wounded thigh of his beloved?
O you who have smelled the lotus with its bees, now endure this, for your stay has been forbidden!
(Abhinavagupta’s *Dhvanyālokalocana*)

If there were unity even when there is a difference in the object—such as in the case of [the thought] "and so forth," where the object resides in a female friend, her lover, and so on—then no distinction would ever exist between blue, yellow, and the like.

For it has been said: "This alone is indeed the distinction, or the cause of distinction, namely, the attribution of contradictory properties and the difference in causes" (from *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvalī*).
[In the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya*:
For denoters there is a dependence upon meaning, but for manifesters there is no such dependence; thus, being a manifester is not the same as being a denoter.

Furthermore, in cases such as "the thicket of reeds" (*vāṇīrakuḍaṅga*), where the expressed meaning, having manifested the suggested sense, comes to rest in its own essential form—there [is the case of suggestion].

Even in the case of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (where the suggested meaning is subordinate), since a meaning that has become the primary intention (*tātparya*) is not denotable by its own word yet enters the path of cognition, to what operation could it possibly belong as its object? Now, one might object: in such instances as "I am Rāma, I endure all," "But by Rāma, who prizes his life, was done toward his beloved what was unbecoming of love," or "That Rāma has attained supreme fame in the worlds through the virtues of his prowess," even the indicated (*lakṣya*) meaning assumes various forms and serves as the cause for specific designations.
That [understanding] occurs; and since its comprehension depends upon the word and its meaning,
as well as upon the context and other factors, what is this so-called "suggested sense" (*pratīyamāna*) that is claimed to be something new?
It is said: even though the object to be indicated (*lakṣya*) may be manifold, it remains strictly determinate, just like the denotation of a word with multiple meanings.
Indeed, it is not possible to indicate [an object] through a primary meaning that lacks a fixed relationship [with that object].

However, the suggested meaning (*pratīyamāna*), by virtue of specific factors such as context (*prakaraṇa*), is manifested as having either a determinate relationship, an indeterminate relationship, or a relationship based on a connection [to another related entity].
"Your lover does not sink here; look for me here every day. O traveler blind by night, do not sink into my bed! (136)
"Your mother-in-law is bathing there; look here during the day, O traveler blind at night, lest you plunge into our bed.
(Hāla’s *Gāthāsaptaśatī* 7.67)
Thus, in the case of *dhvani* where the intended meaning is not the literal one (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*), there is a sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*).
How then can there be indication (*lakṣaṇā*) here?
It has already been established that even in the case of indication, suggestion (*vyañjanā*) must necessarily be resorted to.

Just as denotation (*abhidhā*) depends upon convention (*samaya*), so too does indication (*lakṣaṇā*) depend upon a specific convention consisting of the triad beginning with the sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*).
For this very reason, they say that indication is the "tail" of denotation. Nor is suggestion (*dhvanana*) identical to indication, because it is observed to follow upon that [indication].
Nor is it followed by denotation alone, because it exists even through the operation of indication (*abhidhā*);

nor is it followed by both [denotation and indication] alone, because it is observed even in accordance with syllables that lack expressive power; nor is it followed by sound alone, because it is well known to exist even in such things as a side-long glance from the eye, which is not of the nature of sound. Thus, it transcends the three operations consisting of denotation, intention (*tātparya*), and indication, and is synonymous with "resonance" (*dhvanana*) and other such terms.
The activity is indeed not to be denied.
In that context, in examples such as "the self is here," there is a fixed relationship; in examples such as "whose anger does not arise," there is an unfixed relationship. [As in:
"The Goddess of Fortune, seeing the navel-lotus of Brahmā turned upside down..."
In the inverted act of love,
Lakṣmī, agitated by passion upon seeing Brahmā situated in the navel-lotus,
quickly covers Hari’s right eye.

In such passages as Hāla’s *Gāthāsaptaśatī* 816, there is a "connection of the connected" (*saṃbaddhasaṃbandha*). For here, by the word "Hari," the southern eye is suggested to be of the nature of the sun; by its closing, the setting of the sun is implied.
By that, the lotus closes;
from that, Brahmā is concealed.
This being so, because even the cow’s limbs are no longer visible, the playful dalliance is unrestrained.
The meaning of a sentence alone is the denoted object, graspable by an undivided cognition; and the sentence alone is the denoter.

Even those who say, "([Bṛhaddevī])"— for even by them, having fallen into the realm of ignorance, the conceptualization of words and word-meanings must necessarily be performed— according to their view as well, in the aforementioned examples and the like, the injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth are necessarily suggested (*vyaṅgya*). Now, it might be argued that what is unrelated to the expressed meaning (*vācya*) is not perceived at all, because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of any meaning whatsoever being perceived from anything whatsoever.

And thus, because there is no necessary connection in the relationship between the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), it does not necessarily follow that [the meaning] results in the form of inference—that is, the knowledge of the inferable (*liṅgin*) from a mark (*liṅga*) possessing the three characteristics by virtue of being pervaded and residing in a specific subject (*dharmin*). For instance:
"Go, O traveler, without fear; that dog has been killed today by him."
"O righteous man,
wander with confidence; that dog has been killed today by that proud lion dwelling in the thicket on the bank of the Godāvarī river."

(Hāla’s *Gāthāsaptaśatī* 175 [2.75]) Here, the fact that wandering in this house has been established by the absence of dogs leads to the inference of the absence of wandering on the bank of the Godāvarī, because a lion has been perceived there.

For wherever there is wandering by one who is timid, it is preceded by the perception of the absence of the cause of fear; yet, on the bank of the Godāvarī, a lion is perceived. This is the "perception of what is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

To this it is replied: even a timid person wanders despite the presence of a cause for fear, by the command of a teacher or a master, out of affection for a beloved, or due to some other such reason; thus, the reason [adduced] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, because one who fears dogs does not fear lions due to their heroic nature, the reason is also contradictory (*viruddha*) on the banks of the Godāvarī.
The actual existence of the lion is not ascertained either through perception or through inference,
but rather from a statement;
and yet, that statement possesses no authority.

Furthermore, because there is no necessary connection with the object (*artha*), this reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). How, then, can the proof of the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*) arise from such a reason? Likewise, in the verse beginning with *niḥśeṣacyuta*, those factors such as the falling of sandalwood paste that are presented as indicators (*gamaka*) may also occur due to other causes.
Therefore, since they are mentioned here specifically as effects of bathing, they are not necessarily restricted to sexual enjoyment; thus, they are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Furthermore, the proponent of *vyakti* (suggestion) has stated that these [words] possess suggestiveness when accompanied by the term "low" (*adhama*).
Since "lowness" is not established here by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could there be an inference?
For the proponent of *vyakti*, however, it is no fault that such a meaning is manifested from such a meaning, even in the absence of logical necessity (*upapatti*).

Thus ends the fifth chapter (*ullāsa*) of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, titled "The Determination of the Subdivisions of Suggestive Poetry (*dhvani*) and Poetry of Subordinated Suggestion (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*) as Mixed Types.

Now begins the sixth chapter: Regarding the two types of poetry previously illustrated—those characterized by verbal artistry (*śabdacitra*) and those characterized by semantic artistry (*arthacitra*)—[the following is said]:
In that regard, the presence of both the word and its intended meaning is manifold, depending on whether the quality or the primary element is emphasized.

But it is not the case that when there is verbal artistry (*śabdacitra*) there is a lack of artistry in the meaning (*artha*), nor when there is artistry in the meaning (*arthacitra*) is there a lack of artistry in the word (*śabda*).
And so it has been said:
"Metaphor (*rūpaka*) and other such ornaments have been described by others in many ways as belonging to that [poetry]."
Even the face of a beautiful woman does not shine if it is without ornaments.
Others declare that external ornaments consist of figures such as *rūpaka* (metaphor) and the like;
they desire the grammatical derivation of nouns (*sup*) and verbs (*tiṅ*) to be the ornament of speech.
Regarding this, they say: "This is merely linguistic elegance; such is not the true mastery of meaning.
For us, however, both are desired: the distinction between verbal ornaments and the ornaments of the expressed meaning."
An example of verbal ornamentation (*śabdacitra*) is as follows: First having the hue of dawn-red, then possessing a golden luster,
and thereafter taking on the brilliance of the surface of the cheek of a slender woman languishing in separation;
Then, at the onset of night, the moon— the destroyer of darkness— rises,
possessing the luster of a sliced section of a juicy lotus root.
(Bhavabhūti, *Mālatīmādhava*)
An example of variety in meaning (*arthacitra*) is as follows:
"In this world, whose [mind] would these curls of the long-lashed-eyed women—not to mention their very sight—not disturb? And so too with the wicked."
The base are always characterized by playful deceit;
they never abandon their blackness, as if it were their very crookedness.
(Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*)

Although in all poetry there is ultimately a culmination in the form of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, nevertheless, because a manifest aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is not perceived, these two types of poetry are said to be "non-suggestive" (*avyaṅgya*).

Furthermore, within this category, there are many subdivisions based on the distinctions between verbal and semantic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*); these will be determined in the section on the determination of ornaments.
Thus ends the sixth chapter of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, titled "The Determination of Verbal and Semantic Figures.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
Having defined the nature of poetry (*kāvyasvarūpa*), the author states the general definition of defects (*doṣa*).
The impairment of the primary meaning is a defect, and the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is the primary [meaning], since the expressed sense is its substratum.
Words and other elements are useful for both; therefore, that [defect] applies to them as well.
*Hatirapakarṣaḥ* (the removal of the burden).
By the inclusion of "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "sound and so forth," he states the specific definition regarding the arrangement of phonemes (*varṇa*).

A faulty word is one that is harsh to the ear, deficient in grammatical formation, unidiomatic, or semantically inadequate; it may also have its meaning obscured, convey an inappropriate sense, be redundant, lack denotative power, or be indecent in three ways.
It may be ambiguous, unintelligible, vulgar, or of indirect meaning;
furthermore, it may be obscure, contain an undistinguished predicate, or produce a contradictory understanding when occurring within a compound.
(1) That which is defective due to harsh phonemes is "harsh to the ear" (*śrutikaṭu*). For example:
"When will he, embraced by that slender-limbed woman with the undulating movements of her auspicious side-glances from her house of love, attain the fulfillment of his purpose? (141)
In this regard, [the author] says "the fulfillment of purpose" (*kārtārthya*).
(2) {The mark of decayed refinement} is characterized by a lack of grammatical correctness,
such as: "This [fruit] has a dark belly and is pale, like a *tinduka* fruit that is slightly ripened."
Alas! A secluded spot is found here that can endure the touch of the beautiful hands of the Pulinda hunters.

Therefore, O daughter of the village chieftain, this herd of elephants, piteously entreating you for safety from the frontal lobes [of their heads], implores you: do not cover your pair of breasts with leaves. (142)
(Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*) Regarding the phrase "he entreats" (*anunāthate*):
in examples such as "he entreats for ghee" (*sarpiṣo nāthate*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is prescribed for the root *nāth* only when expressing a benediction (*āśis*).
Regarding the rule *āśiṣi nāthaḥ*,
its meaning here is "to entreat" (*yācana*).
Therefore, it should be read as *anunāthati stanayugam* ("she entreats her pair of breasts").
(3) {Unemployed} likewise, even that which has been handed down by poets is not accepted [if it lacks utility], as in:
"Just as this man of cruel conduct is perceived at all times, so I think he must be a *piśāca* or a *rākṣasa* by fate. (143)

In this context, although the word *daivata* is recorded in the masculine gender according to the rule "the [words] *daivata* and others are used in the masculine," it is not employed as such by anyone.
(4) {Incapable} is that which is recited for a certain purpose, yet he lacks the power to achieve it therein; as in:
"{Having acquired honor by bathing in other sacred fords, he now respectfully approaches the celestial river Ganges.}" (144)
In this [verse] from Ruyyaka’s *Alaṅkārasarvasva*,
the word "strikes" (*hanti*) has the sense of "goes."

(5) {Meaningless} is that which is employed when both meanings are not established; for example: {By her lover, whose hair was reddened by the blow of a foot moist with juice of lac-dye, that innocent girl, trembling with fear upon seeing him, was suddenly kissed. //145//}
In this case (from Śrīvatsalāñchanācārya’s *Kāvyaparīkṣā* 77), by means of the meaning of the word *śoṇita* as "blood," the intended meaning of "being made radiant" is obscured.

(6) {An unusual meaning}: That state which ascetics attain only after a long time through great effort, and which is desired by those performing sacrificial sessions—into that state do the illustrious ones swiftly go, having become the sacrificial animals in the horse-sacrifice of battle. //146//
In this [verse], the word *paśu* (*beast*) manifests cowardice; thus, it is an instance of "inappropriate meaning" (*anucitārtha*).

(7) {Meaningless} refers to a word such as *ca* and so forth, whose sole purpose is to fill out the meter; for example: "O Gaurī, you whose splendor is as white as the pollen of the filaments of blossoming lotuses—O Blessed One, may my desire be fulfilled through your grace. (147)
For here, indeed, is the word *hi*.
(8) {Non-expressive}: For example:

"Embodied beings become submissive of their own accord to one whose anger is never in vain and who destroys calamities; but toward a person who is devoid of indignation and lacks heartfelt affection, no one shows respect out of enmity. //148//
(Bhāravi’s *Kirātārjunīya* 1.33) Here, the word *jantu* is intended to convey the sense of "one who does not give," yet in that context it is not denotative [of that meaning]. Or, for example:
"Alas! That dark-complexioned moon-faced woman, in whom I have seen her..."

This day has been rendered burnt and shrouded in darkness by the pain of that separation; what can we do? If the Creator is ever hostile to our welfare, how is it that this world of living beings does not now become entirely like the night for me? (149)

(Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*) Here, the word *dinam* (day) is expressive of the sense "consisting of light" (*prakāśamaya*). And that which has shifted to another meaning due to association with a prefix (*upasarga*) [is also a case of *vyañjana*].
Just as [the god of love],
whose stalks are his shanks and thighs, is formidable with rows of filaments shimmering from the rays of his nails,
and whose tender sprouts are the spreading luster of fresh lac-dye, and who possesses the bees that are his sweetly tinkling anklets;

Victorious is the foot of Bhavānī, held as a staff, which, while imitating the dance of her husband, surpasses all by assuming the beauty of a lotus born from the pond of the natural, transparent loveliness of her own body.
(Mahimabhaṭṭa’s *Vyaktiviveka*)
In this context, the word "vidadhat" has the sense of "dadhat."
(9) {Obscene language} is threefold because it manifests shame, disgust, or inauspiciousness. For example:
"Who else could withstand the arched brow of that wise man, whose means for success are so great as not to be seen in anyone else? (151) (1)

(Śrīvatsalāñchanācārya’s *Kāvyaparīkṣā*) A certain man, his lower lip bitten by another woman without hesitation though struck by her playful lotus, stood with his eyes closed as if his vision were impaired by the pollen of the flower.
Standing there with her face slightly turned away, offering a breeze with her budding lips, that innocent girl was incessantly kissed by him— whether through delusion or through artifice.
(Amaruśataka 72)
Today, due to the destruction of my beloved wife, the thick and beautiful mass of hair on this fine-haired woman has become unrivaled, its bonds loosened by passion and parted by a gentle breeze.
"When there is one who possesses a flower as his companion, what could this peacock take away?
(Kālidāsa’s *Vikramorvaśīya* 4.22).
In these instances, the words "means" (*sādhana*), "wind" (*vāyu*), and "destruction" (*vināśa*) suggest bashfulness and other such emotions.
(10) {Ambiguous}: For example: "Since your lordship has been embraced by the glory of victory in the next world, please show mercy, placing upon your ear the venerable succession of blessings. (154)
In this [verse], there is a doubt as to whether she is a woman who has been forcibly abducted, or one who is worthy of salutation.
(11) {Uncommon} is that which is well-known only in a specific treatise; for example:
"{For one who possesses a state in which the latent tendencies have been destroyed by the great light of right knowledge, even this [action] being performed would not become a bond of karma. //155//"
(From Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*) (12) {Vulgar (*grāmya*)} is that which exists only in common parlance; for example:
"Your face has a luster transferred from the beloved of the night on the full moon."
"And her waist, with the splendor of a polished golden stone, captivates the mind.
(Śrīvatsalāñchanācārya’s *Kāvyaparīkṣā* 86).
Here, the word "waist" (*kaṭi*) [is an example of a fault].
(13) Some established figurative indications (*lakṣaṇā*) are now being employed by implication, like direct denotations (*abhidhāna*);
some are being used at present, while others are not used at all due to incapacity.
As Kumārila states in the *Tantravārttika* (Pūrva 700):
"That which is prohibited is the figurative (*lākṣaṇika*); for example:
[the moon] 'dear to the night of the full moon shining at the time of autumn'."
"O slender one, it makes your face the recipient of a blow from a palm," [Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*].
Here, by means of the "receiving of a palm-blow," the state of being defeated is indicated (*lakṣyate*).
Now, the connection is that [the fault] is defective only when occurring within a compound; "other" refers to that which occurs elsewhere and that which occurs within a compound.

(14) {Defiled} is that from which the comprehension of meaning is mediated; for example: "O Protector of the Earth, your conduct shines with a beauty comparable to the light emerging from the eyes of Atri. (158)
(Govindaṭhakkura’s Kāvyapradīpa):
Here, the meaning is that [the lake] is [filled] with night-lotuses shining by means of the rising light of the moon born from the three eyes.
(15) {The undiscerned predicate-part}: That [sentence] in which the predicate-part (*vidheyāṃśa*) is not discerned—that is, not indicated as being primary—is an example of this. For instance:

{Of those whose false greatness born of victory over the world was washed away by the streams of blood flowing incessantly from their throats after their upraised heads were severed, and which [streams] had purified the feet of Śiva...}
What is this fruit of their arms— proud with surging arrogance that betrays their desire to make even Mount Kailāsa tremble— if it is merely this exertion in guarding a city?
(Harṣa’s *Nāgānanda* 8)
In this case, the "false majesty" (*mithyā-mahimattva*) is not the subject of restatement (*anuvādya*), but rather the predicate to be enjoined (*vidheya*). For example:
"She repeatedly lowered from her hips the girdle of *kesara* flowers that had slipped away—[a girdle] deposited there by Smara, who knows the proper place, like a second string for his bow. (160)
(Kālidāsa’s *Kumārasaṃbhava* 3.55) Here, it is merely the state of being "second" that is intended as a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
The reading "maurvīṃ dvitīyām" (the bowstring as a second [to the lightning]) is more appropriate. Or, for example:

O fawn-eyed one, among the boons that are sought after, is there even a single thing—beauty, whose body is deformed by three eyes; nobility of birth, which is unperceivable; or wealth, indicated by the state of being naked—that exists in the Three-Eyed One? (Kumārasambhava 5.12)
In this case, it should have been stated as "unobserved birth. Or, for example:
"She who was not released even for a moment—the sole abode for binding the mind that possesses extreme fickleness, like an ocean of bliss."
That anxiety which you have always felt regarding his news now causes you exhaustion; fie, fie upon us!
(Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*)
In this context, "not released" is the predicate to be enjoined; for example: "This is a fresh rain-cloud arrayed for battle, not a haughty night-stalker;
this is a rainbow drawn far back, not his bow."
This too is a sharp downpour of rain, not a succession of arrows;
this is lightning, smooth as gold on a touchstone, not my beloved Urvaśī.
(Kālidāsa’s *Vikramorvaśīya* 4.7)

In this [verse], nothing else is enjoined by way of restating his state of liberation (*amuktatā*). For example: "Fearless, he protected himself; unafflicted, he practiced dharma; free from greed, he acquired wealth; and unattached, he experienced happiness. (164)
In this passage from Kālidāsa’s *Raghuvamśa* (1.21), the concealment of one’s identity and so forth is achieved through the restatement of qualities such as being situated there.
(16) {Creator of Contrary Notions}: For example:
"He whose conduct is as skillful as the rays of the moon—how can we describe that sole friend in misdeeds? (165)
(From the *Śārṅgadharapaddhati*):
Here, while "a friend without purpose" was intended to be expressed, the understanding that arises is "a friend for an improper act. Or, as in:
"Of him who bestows the joy of sight attained after a long time..."
"The beloved suddenly seizes her lover by the neck.
(Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*) Here, "by the throat" (*kaṇṭhagraha*) should have been used instead. Or, for example:
If it was not out of fear that he— whose soul was tranquilized by a continuous flow of genuine compassion— broke the bow of the Blessed Lord, the husband of Bhavānī;
for his son [Skanda] gave cause for universal celebration by slaying Tāraka, who was blinded by intoxication.
"Am I not as dear as Skanda to Skanda himself? Or how have you forgotten that I am your disciple?
(Bhavabhūti’s *Mahāvīracarita* 2.28).
Here, the word "husband of Bhavānī" (*bhavānīpati*) conveys the notion of another husband for Bhavānī. Or, for example:

May that lover of Ambikā protect you— he who, though he has become the mount of even a bull, remains free from pride in the presence of the lion of the Mountain-Daughter. (Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*)
In this context, the phrase "beloved of Ambikā" gives rise to a contradictory notion.
{Śrutikaṭu} (harsh to the ear) pertaining to the past tense, for example:
"She, whose eyes were rippled with thick nectar, is far away; this time has arrived that is fit for loud lamentation. (169)
In this manner, other [cases] as well are to be understood. (Śrīvatsalāñchanācārya’s *Kāvyaparīkṣā* 93)
Setting aside [the defects of] corrupted formation, incapacity, and meaninglessness, these same defects exist in a sentence; some of them also exist in a portion of a word.
Some, but not all; the examples follow in order:
(1) *śrutikaṭu* (harsh-sounding).
He studied the Vedas, sacrificed to the gods, offered oblations to the ancestors, honored his kinsmen,
conquered the group of six internal enemies, delighted in statesmanship, and utterly destroyed his foes.
(Bhaṭṭikāvya 1.2)
May that Duścyavana, who is not engaged [in worldly affairs], grant you a succession of noble descendants,
and may he strike down those who are disapproved by means of defects such as deafness and dumbness. (171)
In this [verse] from Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*,
"duścyavana" refers to Indra, and "aneḍamūka" means one who is both mute and deaf.

O King, your fame—resplendent with the luster of the moon—shines all the more brightly over the lord of the earth who was once constrained by the god whose banner bears the sea-monster and whose arms have arrows as their companions. (3) [This is a verse with its meaning destroyed. (172)
In this [verse] from Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*,
words such as "sāyaka" and so forth are well-known as synonyms for "sword," "ocean," "earth," and "moon," yet they are used here in the sense of "arrow" and so on.
[An example of (4) anucita-artha (inappropriate meaning):
"O Lord, you are a weaver of the multitude of virtues on all sides, while these naked ones sing of your fame in every direction."
Although your fame is beautiful with all its limbs clearly and grandly manifest, white as the autumnal moonlight, it nevertheless wanders here without any covering.
(Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*)
In this case, the word *kuvinda* (weaver), while conveying a different meaning, reveals a disparagement of the person being praised; thus, it is "inappropriate in meaning" (*anucitārtha*).
[5] "Nirarthaka" (Meaningless):
"Having reached the splendor of Viṣṇu, which is as white as a cloud, this Sun (Viṣamāśva) creates..."
In the verse, "The sleep of the thousand-petaled [lotuses], intent on flight," (from Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*),

the words *prābhra*, *bhrāṭ*, *viṣṇudhāman*, *cviṣama*, *aśva*, *nidrā*, and *parṇa* are non-expressive (*avācaka*) of the cloud, the sky, the seven horses [of the sun], the contraction [of petals], and the petals, respectively.
(6) The shameless [and] modest-eyed Kampanā, approaching the king, inspired delusion by displaying various weapons and enthusiasm. //175//

In this context (from Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*), the words "approaching" (*upasarpaṇa*), "striking" (*praharaṇa*), and "bewildering" (*mohana*) are indecorous (*aślīla*) because they evoke shame;
[this refers to the category of] disgust (*jugupsā*).
They eat what has been vomited by others and consume the excrement of others—
those poets whose activity consists in the grasping of another’s meaning.
(Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*)
In this context, words such as "vomiting," "excretion," and "discharge" evoke disgust.
[This is inauspicious.
"I shall go to that abode of my ancestors together with my retinue, where..."

Here, in the intended sense of "the father’s house" and so forth, there is inauspiciousness due to the perception of a cremation ground and the like.
[(7) Ambiguous: "Behold this man, who is intent on the splendor of the celestial abode, who has attained sufficient trembling, who is devoted to seeking [alms], and whose ashes are radiant. (178)

[Unprecedented:
"O friend, for him who possesses superior means and experiences intense spiritual urgency, that firm ground and effort toward attaining what is dear have now borne fruit. (179)

words such as *adhimātropāya* and others are obscure because they are employed exclusively in the *Yogaśāstra*.
[9] Vulgar (*grāmyam*):
This man, his throat filled with betel, prattles nonsense;

[10] Of interpretable meaning:
"O you who have destroyed the dust of sentient beings with feet of cloth and lapis lazuli, you who are unshakable and composed—now reveal the battle of the eyes! (181)
(Śrīvatsalāñchanācārya’s *Kāvyaparīkṣā* 37) Here,

[the phrase] "the earth, its darkness destroyed by the feet of the Jewel of the Sky, has been made immovable" [is used to mean] "awaken the pair of eyes"— this is the fault of *neyārthatā* (indirect or far-fetched meaning).
(11) [Defiled:

Whose mind would not become passionately attached upon beholding the beauty of Dhammillā’s hair—she who has eyes like those of a young fawn—for it is through this unprecedented arrangement that her heart is won? 182.
(Vāmana’s *Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti* 2.1.22) Here,
in the connection "Having beheld the beauty of the braided hair (*dhammilla*), whose mind does not become impassioned?", there is the fault of obscurity (*kliṣṭatva*).
[(12) *Avimṛṣṭavidheyāṃśa* (The element to be predicated is not clearly distinguished): "This indeed is my humiliation—that there are enemies; moreover, that one is an ascetic;

"Fie, fie upon Śakrajit! What is the use of Kumbhakarṇa having been awakened?
And what is the use of these arms, swollen in vain for the purpose of plundering the huts of those who have gone to heaven?
(Harṣa’s *Nāgānanda* 9.55)
In [Abhinavagupta’s *Dhvanyālokalocana*], it should be stated here: "This indeed is the humiliation";
and what is to be restated is merely the state of swelling (*ucchūnatvamātra*).
It is not qualified by the term "uselessness" (*vṛthātva*).
Furthermore, since the arrangement of words here has been made in reverse order, this is a defect of the sentence itself, not of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). Or, for example:
"The glances of her eyes ripple as they meet the corners of her eyes; her eyebrows playfully arch at their curved ends."
"O fortunate one, he who spreads over your body a cloak of bristling hair has arrived.
(Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*) Here, the two words "yo 'sau" (he who) serve only to provide the cognition of what is already being referred to (*anuvādya*).
For instance: the pronoun *tat* (that), when its referent is something previously mentioned, well-known, or experienced, does not require the employment of the relative pronoun *yat* (which).
Examples in order:
"Cowardice is mere policy; valor is the behavior of a beast."
Therefore, he sought success through both of these combined.
(Kālidāsa’s *Raghuvaṃśa* 17.47) Now, this pair has become an object of pity by virtue of its prayer for union with the Skull-Bearer (Kapālin).
She is a digit of the moon, radiant with beauty; you are the moonlight for the eyes of this world.
(Kumārasambhava 5.71) Trembling, her garment slipped away in fear—
Casting those distressed eyes in every direction,
you were not seen by that cruel fire, which, blinded by its own smoke, suddenly consumed you with its ferocity.
In [Harṣa’s] *Ratnāvalī* and [Ānandavardhana’s] *Dhvanyāloka*,

when the word "yat" (which) is employed as following the subsequent sentence, it does not require the explicit mention of the word "tat" (that) which follows the preceding sentence, due to the force of contextual implication (*sāmarthya*). For example:
It was well done by the lotuses that they closed their eyes before the moon, which excels them in loveliness; yet,
as the moon rises victorious over the face of a beautiful woman, they have committed a further act of rashness.
However, a relative pronoun (*yad*) introduced earlier remains expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) without the introduction of its correlative (*tad*),
as in this very verse if the first two quarters were transposed.
But when both are employed, their lack of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) is well established.
Even though there is no explicit mention of grasping (*anupādāna*), by implication both are understood in certain cases; as in:
"Those who spread contempt for us here—do they know anything at all? This effort is not directed toward them."
"Someone of equal nature to me will surely arise;
for time is infinite and the earth is vast.
(Bhavabhūti’s *Mālatīmādhava* 1.7)
In this context, "that which will arise" refers to it;
and thus, if the word "that" were not employed, there would be a state of expectancy here.
Nor is it [the case that] "this."
He states the meaning of that word:

"This spring season has arrived like Hanumān—its beautiful filaments kissed by the wind, its leader the bright orb of the moon, and it is gazed upon by the eyes of women distressed by separation. (190)
For in this case, there is no comprehension of the meaning of that word; or, even if there were comprehension, [it would be flawed].
If that one who is the sole champion in battle against Arjuna Vijaya, assisted by arms as formidable as the trunks of young elephants,
were to be employed by the king in this matter, then the task would be truly accomplished.
(Govindaṭhakkura’s Kāvyapradīpa)
In this case, the word "he" (sa) would be redundant. Now, [if one were to argue]:

"O Lord, for him who perceives this entire circle of objects as a conceptual construction and as Your own body, and for whom the world is filled with his own self, how could there be fear for him who is eternally happy? (192)
In *Vyaktiviveka* by Mahimabhaṭṭa,
it is stated that the word *adaḥ* denotes the meaning of the word *tat* just as the word *idam* does; therefore,
its mention ought to occur in a different sentence right here, and not in that very same place.
