(Bhavabhūti’s *Mālatīmādhava* 5.31)
The state of having a single referent (*ekapadārthatā*) is as follows:

"O you who smear yourself with ashes, may it be well with you! O auspicious one, O rosary of *rudrākṣa* beads! [May there be] a succession of steps adorning the abode of the Beloved of the Daughter of the Mountain!"
Today, by the Lord, gratified by our worship, we are cast into that great delusion called liberation— which destroys the light of the happiness of serving you. (Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*)

Regarding these two offenses, the causes for the former and latter births are, respectively: failing to bow down when an arm falls [upon one], throwing a weapon [at him], and the destruction of the vision of happiness during a great delusion. //114//
Paryāyokta (Indirect Expression) is that speech which occurs without the relationship of signifier and signified;

it is a presentation through a process of comprehension distinct from the relation of signifier and signified, so called because it is expressed by means of a "turn" (*paryāya*), that is, by another manner.
An example: [Example follows]
Beholding whom, even long-established affection for their dwelling was abandoned:
by Airāvaṇa’s pride in his face, and by Indra’s pride in his heart.
(504) (From Meṇṭha’s *Hayagrīvavadha*)
In this case, although it is suggested (*vyaṅgya*) that Airāvaṇa and Śakra have become free from intoxication and pride, it is also expressed by words.
Therefore, that which is expressed is precisely what is suggested;
however, it is not expressed in the same manner as it is suggested.
Just as when a white cow is seen moving, there arises the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that "the white cow is moving.
One conceptualizes exactly what was seen, but not in the manner in which it was seen;
for what was seen as undifferentiated and unassociated is conceptualized through differentiation and association.
The excellence (*udātta*) of a subject is its prosperity; prosperity is the possession of abundance. For example:
"Pearls that had slipped from necklaces whose strings were undone in play, and were swept away by brooms..."

In the mornings, at the edge of the courtyard, the pet parrots of King Bhoja— mistaking the red lac on the slowly moving feet of young girls for pomegranate seeds from afar— peck at them; such is the playful generosity displayed in the mansions of that learned king.
...and it serves as an indicator for great [poets] as well. (Ruyyaka’s *Alaṅkārasarvasva*) ... MKpr-K_115 //
Being a subordinate factor (*aṅgabhāva*) is an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) by implication regarding the object to be indicated. An example:
"This is that very forest, wherein [Rāma], being devoted to fulfilling the command of Daśaratha..."
Dwelling there with only his arm as his companion, Rāma brought about the destruction of the Rākṣasas.
(Rudraṭa’s *Kāvyālaṅkāra* 7.104) And the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) is not present here, because it serves only as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) in this context. (115)
When there is a single cause for the accomplishment of that [effect], and another means of accomplishing it occurs alongside it,
this is conjunction (*samuccaya*).
That is to say, when one means of accomplishing the matter at hand is already established, the occurrence of other means of accomplishment is conjunction.
An example:
"The arrows of Love are difficult to resist; the beloved is far away; the mind is intensely longing;
love is deep; youth is fresh; the vital breaths are exceedingly stubborn; and the family is stainless."

Womanhood is opposed to fortitude, time is a friend to the god of love and intolerant toward the end, and my friends are not clever; how indeed is such a cruel separation to be endured? (Śārṅgadharapaddhati 507)
In this case, it is the arrows of Love alone that cause the inability to endure separation;
the fact of the beloved being situated at a distance and so forth is merely added on top of that.

This very same combination culminates in the conjunction of the auspicious, the inauspicious, and the mixture of the auspicious and inauspicious; therefore, it is not defined separately. For instance:
"The family is stainless, the form is auspicious, the intellect is endowed with sacred learning, the strength of the arms is sufficient, fortune is abundant, and sovereignty is unimpaired."

For these states of being are naturally charming; O King, it is by means of these that people fall all the more into arrogance—and yet, those very things are your goads. (Bhoja’s *Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa* 5.368)
In this case, there is a conjunction of things that exist;
however, in the example mentioned, there is a conjunction of things that do not exist:
"The moon is grey as day; the passionate woman has lost her youth."

A lake devoid of water, a face lacking eloquence despite fine features, a master devoted solely to wealth, a virtuous person who is perpetually destitute, and a rogue who has gained access to the king's court— these seven are thorns in my heart. (509)
In this case, where there is a pale moon as one thorn, there are other thorns as well; such is the conjunction of the beautiful and the ugly.
...but that other [entity] is that which possesses qualities and actions simultaneously.
*Guṇa* and *kriyā*, as well as both *guṇa* and *kriyā*, constitute *guṇakriyā*. The examples in sequence are as follows:
"This army of yours became one that has crushed the entire host of enemies... [etc.]
And though it was pure,
O Lord of Men, the faces of the wicked became soiled.
(Rudraṭa’s *Kāvyālaṅkāra* 7.28)
"This sudden separation from her, brought upon me all at once, is exceedingly difficult for me to bear;
moreover, the days are bound to become delightful due to the absence of the sun's heat because of the rising of fresh rain-clouds.
(Kālidāsa’s *Vikramorvaśīya* 4.10)

O Lord of Kings, your eye, which possesses a splendor like that of a white lotus, has suddenly become turbid toward your enemies; and clearly, the side-glances of calamities have fallen upon their bodies.
(Viśvanātha’s *Sāhityadarpaṇa* 10.85)

Based on the observation of such examples as "He brandishes his sword and spreads his fame," and "You, with sword in hand, are upon the battlefield, while the gods, amidst shouts of 'Bravo!', are in the abode of the gods," one should not state [the conditions] "in different substrates" or "in the same location. (116)
One [thing] in succession among many is a "paryāya" (successive state)...
when one entity occurs or is produced in succession among many, that is a paryāya.
An example in succession is as follows:
O Kālakūṭa, by whom was this successive progression of your abodes taught—
first in the heart of the ocean, then in that of the bull-bannered Śiva?
Now you dwell in the throat, yet again in the speech of the wicked.
(Bhallaṭaśataka 4) Or, for example:
"O slender one, this very passion was previously seen only on your bimba-like lips;
now, O fawn-eyed one, it is observed even in your heart. (Padmagupta, *Navasāhasāṅkacarita* 6.60)

Although passion is in reality diverse, its unity is not contradictory because it is determined as one. [The heart of the beloveds, having a single flavor toward that ornament of the jewel which is the brother of Lakshmi, has been fixed upon Bimba’s lips by the flower-arrowed god. (515)
[In that jewel-ornament which is their glorious brother, their hearts were of one flavor;
yet by the flower-arrowed god, they were placed upon the bimba-like lips of their beloveds.
(Ānandavardhana’s *Viṣamabāṇalīlā*)
Anything other than that is otherwise:
when many [things] occur or are produced in succession within a single [locus], that is the other.
Examples in order:

"The speech of the wicked, charming with its sweetness, first spreads forth like abundant nectar; then, alas, that very same speech reveals itself as the cause of delusion, like the *hālāhala* poison lurking within. (516)
(Śrīvatsalāñchanācārya’s *Kāvyaparīkṣā* 286) "That house has its walls bent; this palace has gained space from the heavens;
that cow is old; these elephants are dark as clouds and trumpeting."
That trivial sound of pestles and this sweet singing of women— what a marvel that in a few days this twice-born man has been raised to such a height!
(Abhinavagupta’s *Dhvanyālokalocana* 3.16)
In this case, because neither the relinquishing nor the taking up of the same single object is intended to be expressed, there is no *parivṛtti* (exchange).
Inference is said to be that statement which expresses the relationship between the probandum and the probans.

The means of proof (*sādhana*) is the three-fold reason (*hetu*), characterized by its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), its positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
The state of being the probandum (*sādhya*) consists in the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) with respect to the subject (*dharmin*). For example:
"Wherever these women with eyes as tremulous as waves direct their eyebrows..."

That these arrows, piercing the vital organs, fall there incessantly— it is true that for them, the wrathful Smara, bearing his command, always runs right in front of them with his bow drawn into a circle and his hand brandishing curved shafts.
In Ruyyaka’s *Alaṅkārasarvasva*:
Since there is no particular strikingness in the variation of the sequence between the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*), it has not been illustrated in that manner. //117//
Parikara (the circumlocution) is an expression of the object of description through significant epithets;
[this applies] by implication to the substantive.
An example:
Those of great prowess, whose wealth was their honor, who were honored for their riches, wielders of the bow who had won fame in battle—
neither did they act in concert against him, nor did they follow a path of dissension.
"They desire to accomplish their dear goals even at the cost of their lives.

(Bhāravi’s *Kirātārjunīya* 1.19) Although the acceptance of "richness of meaning" (*puṣṭārtha*) was established by refuting the claim that it constitutes a defect, nevertheless, there is a distinct aesthetic charm (*vaicitrya*) in presenting many such qualifiers as being centered upon a single subject.
Thus, it is counted among the figures of speech (alaṅkāra).
Circumlocution (*vyājokti*) is the concealment of the true nature of an object that has been revealed by means of a pretext (*chadman*).
*Vyājokti* (the figure of speech of "pretext") occurs when the hidden nature of an object, having been somehow revealed, is denied under some pretext.
Nor is this *apahnuti* (concealment), because here the similarity that resides in both the subject and the non-subject is impossible.
An example follows: [Example omitted per instructions]

Distraught by the interruption of his entire ritual procedure—disturbed by the bristling of his hair and other signs as he was embraced by the hand of Pārvatī, who was being presented to him by the Lord of Mountains—he said with a smile: "Alas! How cool are the hands of the Snowy Mountain!"

May Śiva protect you—he who was seen by the hosts of the mountain’s inner apartments and the circle of Mothers; he whose [divine form] is manifested whether something is slightly asked or not asked at all. (Ruyyaka’s *Alaṅkārasarvasva*) That which is narrated, whether slightly prompted or unprompted, is what is intended here.
That [statement] is traditionally known as a restrictive enumeration (parisaṃkhyā) for the purpose of excluding others of that same kind.

When an object already known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is communicated by a word, and because there is no other purpose, it results in the exclusion of other similar objects, that is *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification).
In this regard, the statement is observed to be either preceded by a question or otherwise;
likewise, in both cases, there is the fourfold division consisting of the perceived nature of the excluded object and its status as being directly expressed (*vācyatva*).
Examples in order:
"What should be resorted to by men? The faultless vicinity of the celestial river. What should be meditated upon in solitude? The pair of feet of the wearer of the Kaustubha gem."
What merit is to be cultivated and what is to be desired? It is compassion;
for by attachment to it, the mind becomes capable of attaining infinite liberation.
(Ruyyaka’s *Alaṅkārasarvasva*)
What is the most steadfast ornament here? Fame, not jewels.
What is the duty to be performed? Noble conduct and virtuous deeds, not vice. What is the unimpeded eye? Intellect, not the physical eye.
Who other than you knows the discrimination between the real and the unreal?
(Viśvanātha’s *Sāhityadarpaṇa* 10.82) Curliness in your mass of hair, and redness in your hands, feet, and lips—
Hardness dwells in her pair of breasts, and tremulousness resides in her eyes.
(Rudraṭa’s *Kāvyālaṅkāra* 7.81) Devotion is directed toward Śiva, not toward worldly wealth; there is an addiction to the scriptures, not to the weapon of desire that is a young woman.
In great men, concern for fame is generally observed, rather than concern for the body.
(Ruyyaka’s *Alaṅkārasarvasva*) //119//
If each subsequent [member] is the cause of each preceding meaning,
then it would be a "garland of causes" (*kāraṇamālā*).
"Each subsequent" means with respect to each following one.

Example:—{Mastery over the senses is the cause of discipline; excellence of virtue is attained through discipline. By excellence of virtue people are won over, for prosperity indeed originates from the affection of the people. //525//}

The statement of a cause together with that which possesses the cause, through non-difference, is the *hetu* [figure of speech]. (Vallabhadeva’s *Subhāṣitāvali*; Śrīvatsalāñchanācārya’s *Kāvyaparīkṣā* 162)
Thus, the figure of speech known as *hetu* (cause) has not been defined [here].
Indeed, forms such as "Clarified butter is life" (*āyurdhṛtam*) can never deserve the status of a poetic ornament (*bhūṣaṇa*), because they lack aesthetic variety (*vaicitrya*). [Example:
"The blooming of lotuses is incessant; there is the intoxication of all the bees; and there is the joy of the cuckoos."
In the verse, "This time is delightful, now causing the world to yearn" (Rudraṭa’s *Kāvyālaṅkāra* 7.83),

the status of this as poetry was established solely by the power of soft alliteration (*komalānuprāsa*), and not through the conceptualization of a figure of speech such as *hetu* (cause); thus, the previously mentioned *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason) itself is the cause [of its poetic quality].
... but through action, they are mutually [dependent].
When two things produce each other through the medium of a single action—
that is, when two objects stand in a state of mutual causality— the poetic figure is named *anyonya* (reciprocity).
An example follows:

The beauty of the swans is enhanced by the lakes, and the beauty of the lakes is enhanced by the swans; these two seem to weigh themselves against one another, yet each considers itself alone to be superior.
These very people merely revile one another for their own sake alone.
(Hāla’s Gāthāsaptaśatī, Nirnaya Sagar Press, p. 953)
In this case, both of these possess a mutual causality by way of accomplishing their respective states of essential glory for one another.
...where the inference of a question is made from the mere hearing of a subsequent statement, or where such a question actually exists. (MK 12.1)
When an answer that was previously considered impossible occurs repeatedly, that is an *uttara*.
First, one type of *uttara* is where the preceding statement is inferred solely from the perception of the reply.
An example: [text missing]
"O merchant, where could we have elephant tusks or tiger skins? Only as long as our daughter-in-law, with her face like a bee, wanders about in the house. (528)
...until the daughter-in-law with her face and locks disheveled is embraced within the house.
(Hāla’s *Gāthāsaptaśatī* 951;
Abhinavagupta’s *Dhvanyālokalocana* 3.17)
The statement of the purchaser, "I desire elephant tusks and tiger skins; give them to me for a price," is inferred by this sentence.
Nor is this *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic cause), because the latter [the answer] cannot logically possess that nature [of being the cause].
For an answer is not the generative cause of a question;

nor is this *anumāna* (inference), because the probandum and the probans are not indicated as residing in a single substratum (*ekadharmī*). Therefore, the answer is better understood as a distinct poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) altogether.
The "other answer" (*aparam uttaram*) is that response which, following the question, takes a form so inconceivable due to its transcending the sphere of the world that it appears impossible.
Furthermore, since beauty is not perceived when these two [the question and the answer] are employed only once, the word "repeatedly" (*asakṛt*) was stated.
An example follows:
What is the uneven course of fate? It is that people are seekers of merit.
What is to be gained? That people are appreciative of virtue. What is happiness? A good wife. What is suffering? A wicked person. (529)
What is happiness? A good wife. What is suffering? That the world is wicked.
(Hāla’s *Gāthāsaptaśatī*, Nirnaya Sagar Press, 975)

In the case of *praśnaparisaṃkhyā* (exclusion by question), the intention lies solely in the exclusion of another; here, however, the rest is upon the expressed meaning itself—this is the distinction between the two.
Even a subtle object, once perceived from some source, is made manifest to another.
Whereby it is described as subtle through some property—
whether from some form, gesture, or other sign— it is subtle and perceivable only by those of sharp intelligence.
An example:

{Seeing the saffron on her neck broken by a continuous stream of sweat-drops trickling from her face, a certain slender friend, revealing the woman's manhood, smiled and drew the outline of a sword upon her hand. (530)}

In this passage from Ruyyaka’s *Alaṅkārasarvasva*, having observed her physical form, a certain woman conjectured her amorous advances toward a man; through her ingenuity, she brought this to manifestation by means of drawing a sword-blade, for it is appropriate that men alone should have swords in their hands.
Or, for example:
"Having perceived that the lover’s mind was fixed on the time of the tryst, the clever woman closed her play-lotus, having subtly conveyed her intention with a slight glance of her eyes. (531)
(From Abhinavagupta’s *Dhvanyālokalocana* 2.36):

Here, the time for the rendezvous, which was desired to be known by a certain woman, is indicated in a playful manner through the closing of the lotus—a gesture that signifies the hour of night and is understood merely by its indicative sign (*iṅgita*).
The progressive excellence that reaches its ultimate limit is the *sāra*.
The "ultimate limit" (paraḥ paryantabhāgaḥ) refers to that which serves as a boundary, because excellence, having ascended through a continuous stream [of refinement], comes to rest precisely there.
An example:
"In a kingdom, the essence is the earth; in the earth, a city; in a city, a palace."
In the palace is the couch; on the couch is the beautiful woman, the very essence of the god of love.
(Rudraṭa’s *Kāvyālaṅkāra* 7.97) //123//
When two properties that stand in a cause-and-effect relationship appear simultaneously in completely different locations, that is the figure of speech known as *asaṃgati* (incongruity).
In this world, it is observed that an effect arises in the very same location as its cause, as in the case of smoke and so forth.

However, when two phenomena, though existing as cause and effect, appear simultaneously in different locations due to some particular excellence, that constitutes "inconsistency" (*asaṃgati*) because of their abandonment of the mutual connection naturally arising from their own nature.
An example is as follows:
"Only he who has a wound feels the pain; people say that is a lie. When there is a tooth-mark on the cheek, the pain belongs to the co-wives. (533)
"The tooth-marks on the bride’s cheek cause pain to her co-wives.
(Hāla’s *Gāthāsaptaśatī* 981).

This is an instance of "subverting contradiction" (*virodhabādhinī*), not actual contradiction (*virodha*), because here the contradiction between the two is manifested precisely through the fact that their lips have been bitten.

In the case of contradiction, however, the state of being contradictory is established—even if not explicitly stated—as residing in a single substratum; for a general rule (utsarga) is determined by excluding the scope of its exception (apavāda).
And thus it has been illustrated as follows: //124//
Concentration (*samādhi*) is a task easily accomplished through the application of auxiliary causes.
When an agent who has been assisted by other means undertakes a task and completes it without difficulty, that is called concentration.
An example follows:
"By good fortune, this thundering of clouds has arisen for my benefit, as I am about to fall at her feet to dispel her pride.
(Daṇḍin’s *Kāvyādarśa* 2.299)
If, in some case, a union [of cause and effect] were possible through equality in terms of fitness (yogyatā), [then it would be valid].

If there is a determination of the relation between these two as restricted to a specific object by way of fitness—namely, that "this is praiseworthy for these two"—then that is *sama* (the Equal), whether it involves a connection between the good (*sat*) or the bad (*asat*).
An example:
"This deer-eyed woman is the touchstone for the excellence of the Creator’s craftsmanship; even the god [Kāma] himself has been surpassed by her peerless beauty."
That their union has occurred by chance in such a fitting manner— this is now the single-sovereign kingdom of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) that has come to pass.
(Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*)
How wonderful, how truly wonderful, oh, how very wonderful and marvelous is this!
By fate, the Creator has been born as an arranger of fitting designs;
for the abundance of the ripened fruits of the *nimba* trees is now fit to be tasted.
And as for that world of *kākāḥ* (crows/cuckoos), which is skilled in the art of devouring this [speech]:
"In some cases, because of extreme dissimilarity, a *śleṣa* (punning connection) does not achieve its proper integration. (Ruyyaka’s *Alaṅkārasarvasva*, verse 536).
The agent neither attains the fruit of the action nor undergoes any misfortune.
When the qualities and actions of the effect are respectively contradicted by the qualities and actions of the cause, this is considered the "unequal" (viṣama) [incongruous] fallacy.
(1) Because the two are absolutely dissimilar, their conjunction is perceived as being simply untenable;
and (2) because when an agent undertakes something, due to the failure of the action, he would not only fail to obtain the desired result, but would even encounter an undesired calamity;
furthermore, (3) even though the effect conforms to the nature of the cause, the qualities and actions of those two would nevertheless become mutually contradictory.
4) That which consists of the opposite of evenness is the uneven, which has four forms.
The examples in order:
"Where is this large-eyed woman, whose limbs are softer even than the *śirīṣa* flower?
And where is this fire of love, harsh as the fire of chaff? (537)
(From Padmagupta’s *Navasāhasāṅkacarita* 1.28):
"The hare, terrified by the son of Siṃhikā (Rāhu), took refuge with the cool-rayed moon;
there, another son of Siṃhikā devoured him along with his refuge."

(Śrīvatsalāñchanācārya’s *Kāvyaparīkṣā* 303) "Immediately upon receiving the touch of his hand, the blade of his sword— dark as a *tamāla* tree in battle after battle— wondrously gives birth to fame as white as the autumn moon, which serves as an ornament for the three worlds. (539)
"O lotus-petal-eyed one, you bestow this intense joy upon me; yet it is by you alone that separation has been produced, which torments my body all the more. (Navasāhasāṅkacarita 1.62)
(Rudraṭa’s *Kāvyālaṅkāra* 9.47) Here, the bestowing of bliss is contradicted by the burning of the body. Likewise:
"By whose vast belly, resting upon the ocean, the worlds were swallowed at the end of the age..."

In such passages as "He was drunk in by the entire eye of a certain city woman, which was agitated with intoxication" (Māgha’s *Śiśupālavadha* 13.40), the quality of *viṣamatva* (unevenness) is to be understood according to its application.
When the two—the supported and the support—are respectively greater than the great, they would be the support and the supported; yet even when they are minute, the latter remains superior.
The dependent is that which is supported, and the support is its substratum.

Even when both of these are large, if— in relation to them— the support and the supported, though small, attain a state of greater magnitude respectively with a view toward the excellence of the subject matter under discussion,
this is the two-fold figure known as *adhika* (the Excessive).
The examples in order:
"O King, how vast is the interior of the three worlds!
For therein is contained the mass of your fame, which is otherwise impossible to contain. (542)

(From Daṇḍin’s *Kāvyādarśa* 2.297) In that body of the enemy of Kaiṭabha, within which the worlds rested at ease when his own self was withdrawn at the end of the age, there was no room for the joys arising from the arrival of the ascetic Manu. (543)
(Māgha’s Śiśupālavadha 1.23) //128//
When one who is unable to retaliate against an adversary resorts to contempt, that contempt is intended as praise for the adversary; this is called *pratyanīka* (counter-argument).

When someone, being unable to directly refute an opponent who is intent on humiliation, instead seeks to disparage another who relies upon that very opponent in order to exalt him—that is called *pratyanīka* (the counter-opponent), because it is equivalent to attacking a substitute for the army.

Just as when an army is to be attacked, some person out of folly attacks another who has become a substitute for it, so too here, when the actual rival is to be conquered, another belonging to that side is conquered; such is the meaning.
Example:
— "O handsome one, you have conquered the form of the god of love, and she is devoted to you;
yet Kāma, as if out of resentment, torments her all at once with his five arrows. (544)
Or as [in Śrīvatsalāñchanācārya’s *Kāvyaparīkṣā* 306]:
"He who, having undertaken a conflict for the sake of restraining the body [of Rāvaṇa], was unable to do him even the slightest harm..."
"Even now, the skillful Rāhu afflicts the moon, which has a form resembling the face of his beloved.
(Māgha’s *Śiśupālavadha* 14.78).
Here, the moon’s status as "his" [Rāhu’s] is due to a connection with a related entity.
When an object is concealed by another object of equal character— whether that concealing object be inherent or adventitious— it is known as *mīlita* (the hidden).

Whatever common characteristic— whether innate or adventitious— exists, by means of which some object is concealed by another object through the very nature of things due to its superior power, that they remember as *mīlita* (the concealed),
and it is considered to be of two kinds.
Eyes tremulous at the corners, sweet and melodious words, a gait slow with the weight of grace, and a face exceedingly lovely— thus,
these qualities manifested spontaneously through the natural playfulness of the fawn-eyed maiden's limbs.

In this case, the arousal of passion (*madodaya*), even though it has taken root, is not perceived; for the tremulousness of the eyes and other such traits of the body are both natural and common to [other states], as they are observed there as well.
(Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*) 546.
Here, the tremulousness of the eyes and so forth are signs of the body that are both innate and universal, since they are seen even in the case of the "great arousal" (*mahodaya*).
Those enemies of yours who always dwell in the caves of the Snowy Mountains, their minds helpless with the fear of your fall upon them,
even as they bear limbs that are trembling and covered in horripilation—
"Alas, even a wise man would not recognize those [tremors] as being caused by fear.

(Ruyyaka’s *Alaṅkārasarvasva*) In this case, however, because the coolness inferred through the power of the context is adventitious, the trembling and horripilation arising from it are likewise characterized as such; furthermore, they share a commonality in that both are observed to occur even in states of fear. //130//
Where an object is either established or excluded, each subsequent one being more excellent than the preceding by way of qualification, that is the two-fold *ekāvalī* (single-string ornament).

When, by means of repetition (*vīpsā*), there occurs the establishment or negation of each preceding thing as a qualifier for each subsequent thing, that is called *ekāvalī* (the single-string necklace) by the wise; it is of two kinds.
The examples in order are as follows:
"In that city, the towns have excellent women; the excellent women have limbs honored by beauty..."
Form is the weapon of the Flower-Armed God, its true charm fully blossomed;
that is not water which does not contain beautiful lotuses. (Padmagupta’s *Navasāhasāṅkacarita* 1.22)
That is not a lotus which does not have bees alighting upon it;
nor is that a bee which does not hum sweetly;
and that is not a humming which did not captivate the mind. (549)

(Bhaṭṭikāvya 2.19) In the preceding [verse], the beautiful women of old are mentioned; by way of their bodily attributes, their beauty is described; by way of their graceful charms, their weapons are described—thus, in this sequence, the qualification is established. In the subsequent [verse], the same logic should be applied even in the case of negation. //131//
Just as there is a recollection of an object according to its experience when something similar to it is seen:
*smaraṇaṃ*...

that object which was at some time experienced as determined by a certain aspect, when at another time a similar thing is seen that serves to awaken the recollection, [it arises] in that very same way.
That which is remembered would be remembrance (*smaraṇa*).
An example:
"The water that was splashed by the waves into the hollows of the deep navels of the tremulous-eyed women..."
The celestial women were reminded of the throat-sounds of lovemaking by the *kuh* cries produced by those [birds].
(Śrivatsalāñchanācārya’s *Kāvyaparīkṣā* 310) Or, for example:
Salutations to the horripilation of Kṛṣṇa, who, having remembered Pañcajanya, placed his lips upon the surface of Yaśodā’s breast grasped by his two hands. (551)
Behold the horripilation of Kṛṣṇa as he remembers the Pāñcajanya conch.
(Hāla’s Gāthāsaptaśatī 974) ...
Illusion (*bhrāntimān*) occurs when there is a perception of something else upon seeing what is similar to it. (MKpr-K_132)
The word "that" (tat) refers to something else that is non-contextual; by means of it, something contextual—such as an object—is understood here as being similar to it.
When such a thing is perceived, the cognition that occurs through its non-contextuality is "the figure of error" (bhrāntimān).
Nor is this a metaphor (*rūpaka*) or a hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) of the first type, because in those cases there is no actual error, whereas here,
since the name is applied according to its literal meaning, that [error] is clearly perceived.
An example:

In a skull, the cat licks its paws, thinking it is milk; the elephant gathers the moonbeams threaded through the gaps in the trees, thinking they are lotus stalks; and at the end of love-making, the woman seizes the rays resting upon the bed, thinking they are her garment.
Ah, the moon, intoxicated by its own radiance, throws this entire world into confusion!
(Bhoja’s *Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa* 3.38;
*Subhāṣitaratnākara* 905)

The *pratīpa* (counter-comparison) consists in the subversion of the standard of comparison, or rather, it should be conceived as the attribution of the status of the object compared (*upameya*) to that very same thing, based on a motive for disparagement.

When the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is discarded by way of rhetorical questioning—on the grounds that the object of comparison (*upameya*) alone is sufficiently mature to bear its burden—it constitutes one form of *pratīpa*.

Furthermore, when the status of being the object of comparison is attributed to that very thing already renowned as the standard of comparison, for the purpose of expressing disregard by intending to introduce another standard of comparison, it constitutes the other form of *pratīpa*, because the object of comparison acts in opposition to the standard of comparison.
Thus, it is *pratīpa* in both forms.

The examples in order: "O King, when you— the abode of beauty, possessed of the majesty of valor, the foremost among the generous, and one whose arm is capable of bearing the burden of the earth— were fashioned by the Creator..."
Was the moon fashioned? Was this sun created?
Was this wish-fulfilling gem produced? And were these mountain ranges made in vain?
(Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*)
"Come here for a moment, O beautiful one; lend me your ear and listen to this which must be said: 'O slender-waisted one, people compare the moon to your face.'"
"O slender-waisted one, the moon is compared to your face by people.
(Hāla’s *Gāthāsaptaśatī* 972).
Here, because the moon—which is being compared by means of the face—possesses far fewer qualities, the comparison is not fully realized; thus, it is "unfit for comparison" (*avaṇijjaṃ*).
Thus, contempt is manifested by words that require explanation. However, in some cases, the very completion of the act of comparison itself serves as the basis for disregard, as in:
"O charming girl, why do you carry this unbearable pride with your pair of eyes?"
"Are there not indeed such blue lotuses in the lakes in every direction?
(Rudraṭa’s *Kāvyālaṅkāra* 8.78).
Here, the very act of making the lotuses the object of comparison constitutes the disregard for them.

In this very manner, it should be understood that when something—due to its possession of extraordinary qualities—is such that even the state of being a point of comparison has never before been experienced, then even the conceptualization of it as such constitutes the *pratīpa* (the inverse) figure; as in:
"O Hālāhala poison, do not be arrogant, thinking 'I alone am the teacher of all things most dreadful'."
But surely, there are many such words of wicked people in this world as those spoken by you?
(Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*)
In this instance, the state of being a point of comparison for Hālāhala poison is described as something utterly impossible.

When the subject at hand is joined with something else through a desire to express equality of qualities, such that they are bound into a single identity, that is traditionally known as *sāmānya* (commonality).

When something that is not of such a nature is intended to be expressed as being so, and it is composed as having become one with another unrelated object while still retaining its own qualities, that is the *sāmānya* type of *udāharaṇa* (illustration), based on the connection of common qualities— e.g.,
"Anointed with sandalwood paste, adorned with fresh strings of pearls..."
With the luster of their faces enhanced by petals of teeth whiter than snow, and wearing beautiful, stainless garments, the *abhisārikās*—
fearless women going to meet their lovers— reach their beloveds' dwellings with ease, as they become indistinguishable from the earth while the moon spreads its light and whitens the world.
(Vāmana’s *Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti* 4.3.10) Here, the whiteness, described as being neither less nor more in both the subject at hand and its other, is the cause of their single essence.
For this very reason, they are not perceived as distinct entities. Or, for example:

If bees had not alighted sportively upon the cheeks of the brides— who possessed a luster equal to the bark of the *vetra* reed— right at the tips of their ears, who would have known the fresh *campaka* flowers?
(Śrivatsalāñchanācārya’s *Kāvyaparīkṣā* 311)

In this case, even a perception of diversity produced by another cause is not able to subvert the non-difference first apprehended, because that [non-difference] has been perceived, and what has been perceived cannot be invalidated by perception.
Without a well-established substratum, there can be no establishment of that which is supported;
[otherwise] a single entity would exist simultaneously in multiple locations, which is a single self existing as many.
When one is performing a different task, [the appearance of] another object that is impossible [to produce],
and likewise the production of that very same thing— this is remembered as the threefold particularity (viśeṣa).
The first type of excellence (*viśeṣa*) is that which expresses the distinguished state of the thing to be supported (*ādheya*), by way of excluding its commonly known [location].
An example:
"Those whose multitude of abundant virtues [endure] until the end of the eon, even for those who have ascended to heaven..."
How could those poets not be worthy of praise whose words delight the worlds?
(Rudraṭa’s *Kāvyālaṅkāra* 9.6).
Even so, that object which exists simultaneously in many places by means of a single nature is the second [type].
An example:— "She dwells in your heart, she alone remains in your eyes, and she is in your words;
O handsome one, where is there room for wretches like us? (560)
"She dwells in your heart, she alone is in your eyes, and she is in your words; O handsome one, where is there room for sinful women like us?
(Hāla’s *Gāthāsaptaśatī* 947)
Even though one might begin something out of impetuosity, to then undertake another task—even if impossible—by that same effort is another distinction.
An example:
"By creating you, whose form is throbbing with wonder and whose blazing majesty is supreme, [the Creator] displayed faultless knowledge..."
"By the Creator, the Mind-born [Cupid], the Earth, Truth, Savitṛ, and Bṛhaspati were created anew.
(Śrīvatsalāñchanācārya’s *Kāvyaparīkṣā* 315). Or, for example:

My wife, my counselor, my intimate friend, and my dear pupil in the practice of the arts— alas, what has not been taken from me by death, which is so merciless in its snatching you away? (Raghuvamśa 8.67)
In every such case, hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) alone stands as the vital essence, for without it, there can be no status as a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*).
Therefore it has been said:
"This is *vakrokti* (curved speech) everywhere; by means of it, the meaning is brought to light."
"The poet must exert effort in this [poetry]; for what ornament is there without it? Thus [it is said].

When an object, by virtue of its conjunction with something possessing exceedingly brilliant qualities, abandons its own quality and assumes the quality of that [other thing], it is called "having the quality of that" (*tadguṇa*).
When an object whose own form is obscured by something else nearby attains a mere appearance colored by the excellence of that other's superior qualities, that is *tadguṇa* (the quality of that).
It is so called because the quality (*guṇa*) of that non-contextual (*aprakṛta*) thing exists here.
An example:
There, the chariots of the Sun, possessing various hues as they flashed all around due to the elder brother of Garuḍa [Aruṇa],
regained their own natural luster through jewels as dark as bamboo shoots.
(Māgha’s *Śiśupālavadha*, 4.56)
Nirnaya Sagar Press.
4.14) Here, the color of the elder brother of Garuḍa (Arjuna) is superior to that of the sun’s horses, and the color of the emeralds is superior to that [of Arjuna]. //137//
If it does not imitate their form, that would be *atadguṇa* (non-imitation of qualities).
However, if this [object], despite possessing the capacity [to do so], does not take on the color belonging to that [other object], then it would be called *atadguṇa*.
An example:—

"O handsome one, although you are white, nevertheless my heart has been colored by you; for even though my heart is filled with passion (*rāga*), you, O charming one, have not become red (*rakta*) within it. (564)
"O fortunate one, although placed within a heart filled with passion, you have not become impassioned.
Here, despite being joined with a mind exceedingly full of passion, he has not attained a state of passion; thus, this is the figure of speech *atadguṇa* (the non-acquisition of a quality).
Furthermore, "that" (*tat*) refers to what is not the subject under discussion (*aprakṛta*), while "this" (*asya*) here indicates what is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*).

Therefore, it should also be understood that when the form of the non-subject is not made to conform to the subject by any cause whatsoever, that is "non-possessing its quality" (*atadguṇa*). For example:
"The water of the Gaṅgā is white; the water of the Yamunā has the luster of collyrium. For one who immerses himself in both—"
O royal swan, that very whiteness of yours is being accumulated, neither decreasing nor increasing.
(Ruyyaka’s *Alaṅkārasarvasva*) Whatever has been established by someone in a certain way, another [establishes] it otherwise. (Madhyamakakārikā 138)
"In the same way, that which is enjoined [contrary to what has been established] is called *vyāghāta* (frustration), according to tradition.

When a certain means (*upāya*) for achieving a particular end has been devised by one person, the deliberate alteration of that very means by another person out of a desire to triumph—because it causes the frustration of the object already accomplished—is *vyāghāta*.
An example follows:"
I praise those beautiful-eyed women who, with their very glance, restore to life the God of Love consumed by the eye of the Three-Eyed One; they are the conquerors of Virūpākṣa.
(Rājaśekhara’s *Viddhaśālabhañjikā* 1.4)
The commingling of these is considered to be their existence here in a state of differentiation.

The *saṃsṛṣṭi* (conjunction) is that which consists in the nature of co-inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*), occurring— according to the possibility of each case— either in the verbal element alone, in the objective element alone, or in both, characterized by mutual independence immediately following the description of these [figures].
Among these, an example of the conjunction of verbal figures (*śabdālaṅkāra*) is as follows:

Another woman, whose beauty was enhanced by the agitation of bees wandering about, lured by the fragrance of her breath, as she moved with eyes rolling like restless waves, produced a sweet tinkling from her girdle. (Māgha’s Śiśupālavadha 6.14)
As for the commingling of figures of sense (*arthālaṅkāra-saṃsṛṣṭi*):
"Darkness, as it were, smears the limbs; the sky, as it were, rains collyrium.
Like service rendered to a wicked man, my vision has become fruitless. (568 [=417])

In the former case, alliteration (*yamaka*) and assonance (*anuprāsa*), being mutually independent, bring about a combination (*saṃsṛṣṭi*); in the latter case, however, it is a similar combination of simile (*upamā*) and poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). As for the combination of verbal and semantic ornaments (*śabdārthālaṅkāra*), it is likewise a *saṃsṛṣṭi*.
"There is no one in this village who can restrain her as she wanders about, her beauty shining with great splendor, plundering the hearts of the young men. (569)
[She] restrains those young men who, plundering her heart, are embracing [her].
(Hāla’s *Gāthāsaptaśatī* 997).
Here, alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and metaphor (*rūpaka*) exist independently of one another.
And their conjunction [is established] because they are both contained within a single sentence, or because they are associated in Vedic usage. //139//
But *saṃkara* (commixture) is the state of being principal and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgitva*) among those [figures] that do not find rest within themselves.

When these very figures, having not attained independence within themselves, assume the relationship of the assisted and the assister toward one another, that is *saṃkara*, because their forms are commingled.
An example follows:
When the emerald *sīmantaratna* jewel has been seized, the golden ear-leaf (*tāṭaṅka*) taken away,

the girdle (*mekhalā*) snatched off, and the pair of jeweled anklets (*maṇitulākoṭi*) suddenly grasped in the forest by the fleeing deer-eyed wives of your enemies— their [lips] are made crimson by the luster of their bimba-like lips.

"O King, the Śabaras do not take away a necklace [of pearls], thinking it to be a string of *guñjā* berries. (Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*) In this instance, the *bhrāntimad* (the figure of mistaken cognition) arises in dependence upon the *tadguṇa* (the figure of "assuming its quality"), and by means of that *bhrāntimad*, the *tadguṇa* becomes a cause of great aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*) for sensitive readers; thus, there exists between these two a relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*). Or, for example:

With the luster of his matted locks, holding a rosary of dark spots in his hand, he appears as pure as one who has renounced the world due to the calamity of separation; on the surface of his forehead, marked by the skull-like stars of the surrounding galaxy, he shines.
"The moon, pale as ashes, moves in the sky like a cremation ground.
(Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*) Here,
as before, four figures— simile (*upamā*), metaphor (*rūpaka*), poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), and paronomasia (*śleṣa*)— are perceived in a relationship of primary and subordinate elements.
In accepting the metaphor (*rūpaka*) that "the spot itself is the rosary," the very fact of its being held in the hand serves as the supporting evidence.

For if this were a metaphor, it would be understood primarily as a rosary whose nature as a "spot" is concealed; and it is precisely that [rosary] which is universally known to be fit for grasping by the hand.
However, through the shadow of a pun (*śleṣa*), the spot is indeed carried [by the hand] in its own physical form.
In the case of the simile "the spot is like a rosary," however, there is a predominant perception of the spot itself.
Furthermore, since its being held in the hand does not exist in reality, even in this primary sense one would have to resort to metaphorical usage (*upacāra*).
And such a confusion (*saṃkara*) is also observed between verbal figures (*śabdālaṅkāra*), as for example:
"This bank shines, having struck down the pride of the foremost Dānavas and possessing a torrential flow that surpasses the currents of the ocean."
"And the elephant herd, with its excellent rutting-fluid ceased, protects the essence of the forest.
(Ratnākara’s *Haravijaya* 5.137).

Here, there is a variety of *citra* (pictorial) ornament consisting of both *yamaka* (rhyme) and *anulomapratiloma* (forward-and-backward palindrome), occurring in two quarters that are mutually dependent.
And when grasping one [of two alternatives], there is no certainty because of the absence of both reason and fault.

Even when two or more figures of speech (alaṅkāras) occur together in a single instance, because of their mutual opposition, they do not abide simultaneously; nor is there any proof for the acceptance of one over the other, or any sublation that would necessitate the exclusion of the other, such that only one could be accepted. This state is characterized by a lack of certainty (niścayābhāva).
The second type is *saṃkara* (commingling), because it implies commingling through conjunction (*samuccaya*).
An example:
"Just as [the ocean] is deep, just as it is filled with jewels, and just as its luster is stainless..."
Why was this ocean not made by the Creator so that it possesses flavorful water,
just as it is deep, just as it is filled with jewels, and just as it has a stainless luster? (573)

(Hāla’s *Gāthāsaptaśatī* 976) Here, since the ocean is the subject under discussion (*prastuta*), there arises the cognition of an unstated object (*aprastutārtha*) through the similarity of its qualifiers. Is this, therefore, *samāsokti* (synecdoche)? Or is it *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), wherein some relevant (*prastuta*) subject is cognized by means of the irrelevant ocean (*aprastuta*) because of their shared qualities?
Thus there is doubt. Or, for example:
"This orb of the moon, which bestows joy upon the eyes, is now becoming clear;
even now, this darkness has its quarters obstructed and is dissolving. (574)

In this [verse from Kṣemendra’s *Aucityavicāracarcā*], is it *paryāyokta* (periphrasis), because the statement "the season that inflames desire is present" is expressed through an indirect turn of phrase;
or rather, is it *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because of the identification (*adhyavasāna*) of the face with the orb of the moon? Or what else?

By pointing to the face with the word "this" (*etad*), it is a metaphor (*rūpaka*) by virtue of superimposing its form [upon the face]. Alternatively, if there is an intention to express their conjunction (*samuccaya*), it is an illuminator (*dīpaka*).
Or else, it is a figure of equal pairing (*tulyayogitā*).
Is this *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation), since at the time of evening there is a comprehension of the face due to the similarity of its qualifiers?

Or rather, is it *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (praise of the irrelevant), because of the context of the face’s purity? Because of such doubt among many [theories], this alone is *saṃkara* (commixture). However, where either a logical proof (*nyāya*) or a defect (*doṣa*) applies, there is no doubt, because one or the other is determined.
Logic consists of being a prover (*sādhakatva*) or being favorable (*anukūlatā*); likewise, a fault consists of being a sublater (*bādhakatva*) or being unfavorable (*pratikūlatā*). In this regard:
"The radiance of her smile spreads grace over the moon of her face, like moonlight.
(Śrīvatsalāñchanācārya’s *Kāvyaparīkṣā* 321)
In this case, the radiance of laughter, which is understood primarily as residing in the face, conforms to it; thus, it supports the simile (*upamā*).
However, since it does not conflict with the moon in that same way, it does not obstruct the metaphor (*rūpaka*).
"O you whose face is a moon, while this [face-moon] exists, that another cool-rayed moon has risen! (576)

In this passage from Harṣa’s *Ratnāvalī* (3.23cd), the fact that the moon’s inferiority is consistent with it and not contrary to the face serves to establish the metaphor (*rūpaka*), rather than subverting the simile (*upamā*).
"O King-Nārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī embraces you most fervently. (577)

In this passage from Udbhaṭa’s *Kāvyālaṅkārasārasaṅgraha*, the act of embracing again serves to exclude the presence of a simile (*upamā*), because an embrace directed toward another’s beloved by one who is himself beloved is impossible.
[May his lotus-foot bring us victory— beautiful...]

In the verse, "The anklets of Ambikā are charming with their tinkling" (*mañjīraśijjitamanoharam ambikāyāḥ*), the tinkling of the anklets is incompatible with the lotus because it is impossible [for them to exist there]; thus, this constitutes a sublation of the metaphor (*rūpaka*) with respect to the lotus, but not with respect to the foot.

It is stated that "conducive" (*anukūla*) is the prover (*sādhaka*) of the simile, because the subverting factor (*bādhaka*) which suppresses the injunction is perceived as being more intense than that [simile].
In this same manner, the wise should investigate other cases as well. //140//
Two figures of sound and meaning are clearly established together in a single object;
and they are manifestly situated within the very same word.
When both sound and sense ornaments attain a state of coexistence, that too is another type of *saṃkara* (commixture).
An example:
{The solar orb, whose filaments of rays shine clearly...}
Then the day-lotus, with its broad pericarp, contracted; it was a lotus whose opening of petals— the cluster of the eight directions—
had been enveloped in darkness by the swarm of bees.
In this passage from Ratnākara’s *Haravijaya* (19.1), both metaphor (*rūpaka*) and alliteration (*anuprāsa*) are combined within a single word.
...therefore, it is proclaimed as having three aspects. // MKpr-K_141 //

Thus, this *saṃkara* (commixture) has been explained as being of only three types, because it is established through the relationship of the favored and the favorer, through doubt, and through being expressed by a single word.

However, it cannot be explained in any other way due to the infinity of its subdivisions. Thus have been presented the figures of speech (*alaṅkāras*) which possess a threefold nature by virtue of residing in the word, the meaning, or both.

But why this restriction— that although these [figures] are equally causes for the excellence of poetic beauty (*kāvyasobhātiśaya*), some figure belongs to the word, some to the meaning, and some to both?

It has already been stated that in poetry, with respect to the determination of defects, merits, and figures as residing in the word, the meaning, or both, only positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) are effective, since there is no other cause.
Therefore, whatever ornament follows the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of another, that is established as an ornament belonging to that [other].

And thus, just as *punaruktavad-ābhāsa* and *paraṃparita-rūpaka* are ornaments of both [word and meaning] because they follow the presence of both, so too should *śabda-hetuka-arthāntaranyāsa* and others be regarded.
However, because the diversity of the meaning (artha) appears there with such intensity,
these [figures] have been defined among the ornaments of the expressed (vācyālaṅkāra), regardless of the actual state of things.

Even if one were to maintain the view that "whatever ornament rests upon something, that is the ornament of that thing," one must still rely solely on positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), because without resorting to those, no specific relationship of substrate and superstratum (āśrayāśrayibhāva) can exist; therefore, the mutual distinction among ornaments is best established precisely through the aforementioned grounds. 141.
Although some of these faults may occur as appropriate, they are included within those already mentioned; therefore, they have not been explained separately.

For instance: the three defects of alliteration—namely, lack of conventional usage (*prasiddhyabhāva*), futility (*vaiphalya*), and conflict with the poetic style (*vṛttivirodha*)—do not transcend, respectively, contradiction with convention (*prasiddhiviruddhatā*), lack of significance (*apuṣṭārthatva*), and discordance of phonemes (*pratikūlavarṇatā*), because they are of the same nature as those [three]. Examples in order:

The Wheel-bearer [Viṣṇu] guards the row of wheel-spokes, Hari likewise guards the horses, Dhūrjaṭi [Śiva] guards the tips of the banners on the pole, Varuṇa guards the axle, Kubera guards the tip of the pole,
and the host of gods guards the speed of that one who is eternally intent upon benefiting the world.
"May that chariot of the sun, which daily praises [him] while overflowing with joy, protect you!
(Mayūra’s *Sūryaśataka* 71).

Here, the praise is performed according to a specific restriction of agent and object solely for the sake of alliteration (*anuprāsa*), and since it is not perceived as such in the Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and other sources, there is a contradiction with established tradition (*prasiddhivirodha*).
"Speak, O young woman, whose moon-like face is beautiful and distills bliss, you who utter playful words with grace: if you are going to the lover’s abode, then what of yours belongs to me?
(Rudraṭa’s *Kāvyālaṅkāra* 2.22)

The wandering about of her red feet— accompanied by the resonance of tinkling jeweled girdles and the incessant jingling of lovely anklets— produces a restless longing for no other reason. (582 = 207) (Rudraṭa’s *Kāvyālaṅkāra* 2.23)
In this case, no charm whatsoever is perceived upon reflection regarding the expressed meaning; thus, the futility of the alliteration consists precisely in its lack of a significant purpose.

In the verse beginning with *akuṇṭhotkaṇṭhayā*, the ostentation of harsh-sounding phonemes (*paruṣavarṇāḍambara*) contradicts the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) according to the method previously stated; thus, the alliteration of harsh sounds (*paruṣānuprāsa*) here constitutes a contradiction of style (*vṛttivirodha*) precisely because of its discordant phonemes.
The fault of non-application (*aprayuktatva*) consists in the lack of symmetry when there is a lack of correspondence across three feet of a *yamaka*. For example:

“Like the jewel of a serpent, like a river infested with crocodiles and full of deception, those full of deception forcibly drag away the heart of a living being, even one who has determined their ultimate futility. (583)
In Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*:

In the case of a simile (*upamā*), a deficiency or excess in the genus (*jāti*) or the measure (*pramāṇa*) of the object of comparison (*upamāna*) constitutes the fault of "inappropriateness of meaning" (*anucitārthatva*). However, when deficiency or excess pertains to the attribute (*dharma*), they do not deviate from [the faults of] "deficiency of words" (*hīnapadatva*) and "excess of words" (*adhikapadatva*) respectively.
Examples in order:
"A most reckless deed has been committed by you, as if you were outcasts.
(Vāmana’s *Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti* 4.2.9)
This sun shines like a spark of fire.
(Vāmana’s *Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti* 4.2) This cakravāka bird, seated upon a lotus, shines resplendently.
At the beginning of the Yuga, the Blessed Lord Brahmā was as if desirous of creating living beings.
(Bhāmaha’s *Kāvyālaṅkāra* 2.25;
Vāmana’s *Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti* 4.2.11)
Your navel is like the underworld (pātāla), your breasts resemble mountains,
and this braid of hair, moreover, is like the descent of the Yamunā (Kālindī).
(Vāmana’s Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti 4.2.11)
And here, since the subject under discussion is compared to outcasts and the like, it is excessively degraded; thus, this is the figure *anucitārthatā* (inappropriateness of meaning).
That sage, marked by his girdle of muñja grass and wearing a garment of black antelope skin,
shone like the sun embraced by a portion of dark clouds.
(Vāmana’s *Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti* 4.2.9)

In this case, because the attribute corresponding to the girdle (mauñjī)—namely, the characteristic of lightning—is not expressed by any word, there is the defect of "deficiency of words" (hīnapadatva).
Clad in yellow garments and grasping his Śārṅga bow, Kṛṣṇa assumed a form both charming and formidable,
like a cloud at night endowed with lightning and a rainbow as it is joined by the moon.
(Bhāmaha’s *Kāvyālaṅkāra* 2.58)

In this case, since the object of comparison (upamēya), such as the conch shell and so forth, is not specified, the mention of the moon is superfluous; thus, there is the fault of "superfluous words" (adhika-pada-tva).

Even a difference in gender or number between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) constitutes a breach of uniformity if it causes the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) to take on a different form. In that case, since the possession of that attribute is understood to belong to only one of the two, the status of being either the standard or the object of comparison is perceived—by means of the implied attribute—as belonging only to that [one] along with its qualification. Thus, because the intended meaning is not clearly sustained, this constitutes the fault of "broken uniformity" (*bhagnaprakrama*). For example: [Example omitted as per instructions]
"Alas, you have fallen from my hand like a wish-fulfilling gem; fie upon my wretched fortune!
(Rudraṭa, *Kāvyālaṅkāra* 11.20) "O King, I have eaten barley-meal, as pure as a virtuous wife. (11.21)

(Śrīvatsalāñchanācārya’s *Kāvyaparīkṣā* 334) However, where there is diversity in gender and number, if the word denoting the general [quality] does not undergo a change in its two-fold form, then this fault does not arise; for in both cases, it possesses a nature capable of being a pervasive concomitant (*anugamaka*).
As, for example:
Renowned for his priceless virtues, like the great ocean for its jewels;
he who possesses a sweetness of character unequaled by other women, yet bears a dress unlike theirs. (Śrivatsalāñchanācārya’s *Kāvyaparīkṣā* 335)
They attained supreme beauty, as if they were his own graceful movements.

(Śrīvatsalāñchanācārya’s *Kāvyaparīkṣā* 336) Even when there is a difference in tense, person, mood, and so forth, if the cognition does not attain a state of rest due to its unimpeded nature, this too is pervaded by the fault of broken uniformity (*bhagnaprakrama*). For example:
From Kakutstha, Kumudvatī obtained a son named Atithi, just as consciousness attains clarity from the final watch of the night. (Raghuvaṃśa 17.1)
In this case, the volition attains clarity but does not lose it again; such is the distinction of time.
[Her] form is purified by the excellence of a fresh bath, and she is lovely with the shimmering edges of garments beautiful with safflower dye.
You shine like a creeper sprouting from a branch of young coral, as you worship the god whose banner is the sea-monster.
(Harṣa’s *Ratnāvalī* 1.20)

In this instance, there is a difference in person (*puruṣabheda*) due to the transposition of the predicate residing in the person being addressed—namely "the creeper shines"—into the subject that is not being addressed, as in "you do not shine. [Example:
"May your fame flow forever like the Gaṅgā.
(Śrivatsalāñchanācārya’s *Kāvyaparīkṣā* 339)
And in such cases as "the Gaṅgā flows," [there is no comparison] because the injunction—which consists in the instigation of what has not yet begun—is expressed as "let it flow";
furthermore, since other such meanings residing in the standard of comparison (upamāna) are impossible, there is a distinction from injunction and the like.

Now, it may be argued that when a comparison is completed by resorting to some other attribute— whether that attribute is explicitly uttered or merely implied— there is no discrepancy regarding time and so forth, because the object of comparison (the *upameya*) is connected with its own inherent attribute (*prakṛtadharma*).
This is true even in cases where the comparison is established solely through a common attribute (*sāmānyadharma*) that has been explicitly mentioned.

It is understood, for example, that "this person speaks the truth just like Yudhiṣṭhira. In that case, we shall understand the meaning as: "This speaker of truth speaks the truth, just like Yudhiṣṭhira. Nor should a redundancy be suspected in the expression "a speaker of truth speaks the truth," because—just as in the case of "he nourishes his prosperity"—the meaning is understood to be: "By speaking the truth, he is a speaker of truth, just like Yudhiṣṭhira."

This is true; however, while this justification holds for the established usages, it is not entirely faultless because it obstructs the comprehension of the subject matter at hand—of this, the discerning mind alone is the authority here.
Even dissimilarity (*asādṛśya*) and impossibility (*asaṃbhava*) in a simile result ultimately in the fault of "inappropriateness of meaning" (*anucitārthatā*). For example:
"I string together the moon of poetry, which has rays in the form of extensive meanings.
(Vāmana’s *Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti* 2.4.16)

In this instance, no similarity whatsoever is perceived between the poem and the moon, or between its meanings and the moon's rays; thus, there is the fault of "impropriety of meaning" (anucitārthatva).
[For example: "From his mouth, as it were, gleaming arrows fell, situated within the circle of his bow."
Like streams of water blazing forth from the sun that has reached midday and is surrounded by a halo.
(Govindaṭhakkura’s *Kāvyapradīpa*)
Even here, the depiction of flaming streams of water issuing from the solar disc as being impossible fosters nothing but a lack of propriety.

Even in the case of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), only words such as *dhruvam*, *iva*, and so forth are capable of expressing the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*), whereas the word *yathā* is not; for this word alone is sufficient only to convey similarity (*sādharmya*), and since that [similarity] is not intended to be expressed here, its inability [to express the required sense] constitutes the fault of being non-expressive (*avācakatva*).
Just as a dark blue lotus bud emerged from the heart of a long pond, appearing as if it had shrunk out of apprehension toward the cleverness of a woman’s eyes.

(Śrīvatsalāñchanācārya’s *Kāvyaparīkṣā* 340) Even that which is imagined is like something non-existent, because it is devoid of any real form. Therefore, the employment of a corroborative generalization (*arthāntaranyāsa*) to support it is as utterly improper as a painting on the surface of the sky; thus, this [corroborative generalization] lacks a valid object.
The fault lies precisely in the inappropriateness of the meaning. For example:

"He who protects the darkness hidden in caves from the sun, as if it were afraid of the day—surely, even when a lowly person has approached, there is an excessive sense of 'mine' in those of high station. (600)

(Kālidāsa’s *Kumārasambhava* 1.12) Here, since it is impossible for insentient darkness to feel fear of the sun, how could there even be protection from it provided by the mountain? However, as this [darkness] appears in a form that is merely imagined, no logical inconsistency arises; thus, any effort to justify it is entirely futile.

Since the *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation) reveals the unexpressed object of comparison through the power of common attributes alone, there is no purpose in restating it here; thus, its non-inclusion constitutes the fault of "lack of significance" (*apuṣṭārthatva*) or "redundancy" (*punarukta*). For example:
"When the hot-rayed sun touches the quarters with his rays, as if with a beloved woman whose fever has intensified..."
[The day’s splendor] remained for a long time with its beautiful radiance, yet without embracing a slender form.

(Ratnākara’s *Haravijaya* 3.37) Herein, by virtue of the similar adjectives and the specific identification [of the subjects], the sun (*tigmaruci*) and the quarters (*kakubh*) are manifested as the hero (*nāyaka*) and the heroine (*nāyikā*), respectively.
Likewise, since the beauty of the summer day will also serve as a rival heroine (*pratināyikā*), what is the point of employing the word "beloved" (*dayitā*)?

The domain of *śleṣopamā* (metaphorical simile), however, is that case where, even when the common attributes are present, there is no such recognition [of similarity] without the explicit mention of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). As in:

"And she herself, copper-red like a sprout and resplendent with shining rays, grants the desired fruits to those who seek them, like the dawn twilight which grants the desired fruits to those who do not sleep. (602)

(Udbhaṭa’s *Kāvyālaṅkārasārasaṅgraha* 4.15) Even in the case of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), the object of comparison (*upameya*) is understood through this very same method; it should not be subjected to the indignity of being explicitly stated again. As in: "When birds were summoned, the mosquito was not prevented from coming forward."
Even while dwelling in the midst of the ocean, the *tṛṇamaṇi* (grass-gem) bears the luster of jewels;
even a firefly does not tremble to move in the midst of luminous bodies.
Fie upon that insentient commonality which, like a master who has not grasped the inner essence of reality, remains indifferent!
(Bhallaṭaśataka 67) Here, since the insentient master is manifested by means of a specific generalization that is not the subject at hand, it is certainly not appropriate to state it again.

Thus, these defects of ornamentation, as well as others of a similar kind that may possibly occur, are subsumed under the very categories of defects previously mentioned; they do not merit separate treatment. This definition of poetry is therefore complete. //142//

"That this path, though distinct for various learned scholars, appears as a single undivided form is not surprising; for in that case, the cause is simply the perfectly executed composition itself. Thus ends the tenth chapter of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, titled "The Determination of Figures of Sense" (*Arthālaṅkāranirṇaya*).
And thus the Kāvyaprakāśa is completed.
This treatise is completed.
